catalogue.name: Dates & Formatting
catalogue.tagline: Format, parse and time-zone a date once, so the server and the page agree.
catalogue.why: Every case, claim and permit carries dates that are read by a person and stored by a machine, and the two must not disagree. Without this, a developer writes toLocaleDateString in a page and a hand-rolled ISO slice in a flow, and the same instant renders as two different days for a user in another office. One call each for render-with-an-explicit-pattern, render-in-a-named-zone, parse, and canonical storage form.
catalogue.risk: Every function returns or takes a Date object, and a Date in a flow's context round-trips through JSON differently in the preview interpreter than in the exported Node server — so a stored value must go through To ISO String, and that discipline is unenforced. Patterns are date-fns tokens, where YYYY means week-year and yyyy means year: the classic silent off-by-a-year every New Year's Eve. Time-zone names resolve through Node's ICU data, and a slim base image built without full ICU falls back to UTC silently rather than failing. Verified working under Node 20 CommonJS: date-fns 4.1.0 and date-fns-tz 3.2.0 both require() and type-check; formatInTimeZone(2026-09-10T00:00Z, 'Asia/Singapore') returned 2026-09-10 08:00.

functions.description: Render a date with an explicit pattern, so a letter, a page and an export all read the same.

functions.name: Format In Time Zone
functions.description: Render an instant in a named IANA zone — the one that matters when the server runs in UTC and the agency does not.

functions.name: Parse ISO Date
functions.description: Turn an ISO 8601 string from a form, a CSV or an API into a date.

functions.name: To ISO String
functions.description: The canonical string form for storage and for an API response. Pair it with every function that returns a Date.

functions.name: Start Of Day
functions.description: Midnight of that date — the left edge of a day filter.

functions.name: End Of Day
functions.description: The right edge of a day filter.

functions.name: End Of Month
functions.description: Period close, reporting cut-off, billing boundary.

functions.name: Time Ago
functions.description: "3 days" for a case-age column or an activity line.

functions.name: To Time Zone
functions.description: An instant re-expressed as wall-clock time in a zone, for date arithmetic that must happen on the local day.

functions.name: From Time Zone
functions.description: Wall-clock text a person typed in their zone, back to a real instant — the conversion an appointment form always gets wrong.

catalogue.name: Lists, Groups & Summaries
catalogue.tagline: Sort, group, de-duplicate and total rows — the list operations behind every console and dashboard.
catalogue.why: Every list page sorts by two keys, every dashboard groups by status and counts, every bulk send needs rows chunked, and every import needs the rows that are new. Written by hand each is ten lines of reduce inside an expression that nobody can read a month later. These make each one node with named inputs, which is also the difference between a flow a reviewer can follow and one they cannot.
catalogue.risk: Group By returns a keyed OBJECT and the composable canvas repeats over ARRAYS, so the common case costs two nodes — Group By then Group Entries — and a developer who forgets gets a page that renders nothing with no error. Iteratee arguments arrive as {{= ["dueDate"] }} expressions, so a mistyped field name sorts by nothing and fails silently rather than erroring. Everything is in memory: these are for a page of rows, not a table scan, and Sum By over an unbounded Query is the wrong shape however well it reads. Pinned at lodash 4.17.21 with @types/lodash 4.17.x because the types line still trails the runtime; verified requiring and grouping under CommonJS.

functions.name: Order By
functions.description: Sort with a direction per field — the list page's two-key sort.

functions.name: Group By
functions.description: Group rows by a field into a keyed object.

functions.name: Group Entries
functions.description: Turn a grouped object into [key, rows] pairs so a list can repeat over it. Call it after Group By, every time.

functions.name: Key By
functions.description: Index rows by id for O(1) lookup across a join done in the flow.

functions.name: Unique By
functions.description: De-duplicate rows on a field — the bulk-upload guard.

functions.name: Difference By
functions.description: Rows in the first list that are not in the second, by a field — what an import is actually adding.

functions.name: Chunk
functions.description: Split rows into fixed-size batches for paged sending or bulk writes.

functions.name: Sum By
functions.description: Total a numeric field, for a claim, an order or a tile.

functions.name: Count By
functions.description: Counts per value — the status breakdown behind every summary bar.

functions.name: Max By
functions.description: The row with the largest value of a field — the latest event, the biggest line.

catalogue.name: Record Detail & Fields
catalogue.tagline: The read half of a record page — labelled fields, typed values, before/after diffs, masked and copyable values.
catalogue.why: Half of a case-management screen is not a form: it is the record as read-only fields, the request as 'what changed', a payload as JSON, a hierarchy as a tree, and one or two values that must not be shown to everyone. Each is rebuilt slightly differently on every project, and the diff in particular is the single thing an approver actually reads before clicking Approve.
catalogue.risk: DescriptionList takes an array of objects assembled in an expression, which is the least pleasant binding in a low-code inspector — a comma-separated field list over a bound record would be friendlier and should be prototyped before this ships. JsonViewer and TreeView recurse, and a self-import is a cycle that CODE-006 refuses, so each recurses through an inner function in the same file: valid, but long, and long code components are what the platform's own page rules push back on. RichTextView renders HTML it did not sanitize — it is only safe when the HTML came from the Markdown library's Sanitize HTML on the server, and nothing enforces that pairing. MaskedValue's onReveal is a convention, not a guarantee: the component cannot make anyone record the audit event.

components.name: DescriptionList
components.description: The labelled field panel every detail page is mostly made of: two columns on a laptop, stacked on a phone.
components.notes: A <dl> on a CSS grid. A missing value renders an em-dash in text-muted-foreground so an empty field reads as deliberate rather than as a rendering bug.

components.name: FieldValue
components.description: One labelled value formatted by its declared type — the prop that stops an ISO timestamp reaching a screen a citizen reads.
components.notes: Intl.NumberFormat and Intl.DateTimeFormat only — no date or money library in the browser. Booleans render a lucide Check/X pair; contacts render mailto:/tel: anchors.

components.name: FieldDiffTable
components.description: What changed in this request — field, before, after — with unchanged fields hidden by default.
components.notes: A key-by-key comparison, not a diff algorithm. Old value text-muted-foreground with a strikethrough, new value text-foreground, changed rows carry a left border — two channels, so the direction survives a greyscale print of the case file. Pairs with the audit library's Field Changes.

components.name: FieldDiffRow
components.description: A single before → after pair, for embedding in a feed or an audit row.
components.notes: Exported separately so the timeline library's AuditTrail renders a change identically instead of inventing its own arrow.

components.name: JsonViewer
components.description: An integration payload or an agent transcript, explorable rather than dumped.
components.notes: Recursion through an inner function component in the same file — never a self-import, which validation refuses as a cycle. A collapsed object previews as '{3 keys}' so a deep payload stays scannable.

components.name: TreeView
components.description: Hierarchies — org units, category codes, document folders — with keyboard navigation.
props: nodes (Array<{id, label, children, count?, icon?, disabled?}>)
components.notes: Rows are buttons carrying role=treeitem, aria-expanded and aria-level with arrow-key movement — the part hand-rolled trees skip and an accessibility audit always finds. A 1px guide rule per level keeps deep nesting traceable.

components.name: MaskedValue
components.description: A restricted field, revealed on purpose and on the record.
components.notes: Never unmasks itself: revealed is controlled by the page, so the parent can await an audit write before flipping it. Optional reason prompt on @radix-ui/react-dialog; the value is font-mono so a revealed identifier reads character by character.

components.name: CopyableValue
components.description: The reference number a user will paste into a ticket or an email.
components.notes: lucide Copy swapping to Check for 1.5s, over navigator.clipboard, falling back to selecting the text node where the clipboard API is unavailable — an intranet on plain http, which this audience has more of than it should.

components.name: RichTextView
components.description: Case notes or a knowledge article stored as markdown and rendered to HTML on the server.
components.notes: A hand-written prose scale in Tailwind arbitrary variants ([&_h2]:text-lg, [&_ul]:list-disc, [&_th]:border-b) because the typography plugin is not available. Trusts its input: pass only HTML that went through Sanitize HTML.

catalogue.name: Status, Priority & SLA
catalogue.tagline: A record's state said the same way on every screen — badges, priority, countdowns, handling markings.
catalogue.why: Every case, claim, requisition and ticket has a state, and in practice each screen invents its own colours and words for it. One tone map applied by a component means 'Awaiting approval' looks identical in the list, the detail header and the task inbox, and a status added to the model does not mean editing six pages. It also enforces the rule these apps are audited against: state is never colour alone.
catalogue.risk: The built-in word→tone map is a guess about someone else's domain — a registry where 'Closed' is success and one where it is failure both exist — so it must be overridable per instance, and developers will forget on half their screens; a per-app tone map is what this really wants and a code component has nowhere to put one. SlaIndicator's per-minute interval is fine for one badge and wasteful in a 200-row table, where one shared clock would be right and there is nowhere to put it either. timeZone must be an explicit prop rather than the browser's, or a reviewer in another office sees the wrong due date — a bug that never appears on the developer's machine. Classification levels map onto theme tokens (muted → secondary → primary → destructive), so the ordering reads but the exact colour of a paper handling scheme will not match.

components.name: StatusBadge
components.description: A record's state as a word, an icon and a reserved tone.
components.notes: Tone resolves from the prop first, then a built-in map of the words these apps use (draft, submitted, pending, in review, approved, rejected, on hold, closed, overdue). Soft fill is color-mix(in oklab, currentColor 12%, transparent) so ink and fill move together and dark mode needs no dark: variant. Always word plus icon.

components.name: StatusDot
components.description: A compact state marker for dense tables and list rows.
components.notes: An 8px round span with an sr-only label, so a screen reader gets what a sighted user gets from the colour. pulse is reserved for genuinely live states.

components.name: PriorityChip
components.description: Low / Medium / High / Critical, with the icon doing as much work as the colour.
components.notes: lucide ChevronsDown / Minus / ChevronUp / AlertTriangle ramping alongside muted → warning → destructive, so priority survives the greyscale printing a case file gets.

components.name: SlaIndicator
components.description: Time remaining against a due date, in words, going warning then breached.
props: status (stops the clock when closed or paused)
components.notes: Intl.RelativeTimeFormat gives the phrase with no date library; unit selection is a threshold table over the millisecond delta. A paused or closed status freezes the clock rather than counting into a breach that never happened — the difference between a useful indicator and a wall of false red.

components.name: SlaMeter
components.description: The same clock as a bar from start to due, with a tick at the deadline.
components.notes: Inline SVG: one track rect, one fill rect with a computed width attribute, one tick line. SVG geometry is attributes, not class names, so nothing dynamic touches Tailwind. now is a prop, never Date.now(), so the canvas renders it deterministically.

components.name: StatusSummaryBar
components.description: A queue's composition above the table it filters — 32 open, 8 overdue, 4 on hold.
components.notes: A flex row of divs with flex-grow per value and gap-[2px] — flexbox does the proportional arithmetic, so it reflows at any width with no measurement and no re-render. Clicking a segment emits the status, which turns it from decoration into a filter.

components.name: StatusLegend
components.description: The tone map declared on the page, so badges are not the only explanation.
components.notes: Dull, and the thing that makes a page of colour-coded rows defensible in an accessibility review.

components.name: ClassificationBanner
components.description: A handling banner across the top of a page or a printed document, so a screenshot carries its own marking.
components.notes: Levels map onto theme tokens in increasing weight; uppercase tracking-wide text-xs. Sticky uses top-0 z-40 over the page's own background.

components.name: RetentionBadge
components.description: How long a record is kept and what that makes it — active, due for review, expired, or under legal hold.
components.notes: lucide Clock / AlertTriangle / Trash2 / Lock. Hold always outranks expired and renders with the lock, since a record under hold must never read as disposable.

catalogue.name: Working Days & Deadlines
catalogue.tagline: Weekend-skipping SLA arithmetic and calendar maths for retention and appeal windows.
catalogue.why: Two deadlines run through every regulated app and both get computed wrong by hand. An SLA — 'respond within 5 working days' — is written as addDays(date, days * 1.4) in a hurry. A retention date — 'destroy 7 years after the case closes' — needs month-end and leap-year behaviour and is the field a records manager audits first. Each of these is one correctly-implemented call.
catalogue.risk: date-fns knows WEEKENDS and does NOT know PUBLIC HOLIDAYS, which for a public-sector deployment is most of the reason a working-day calendar exists — an SLA is wrong by up to a fortnight over Christmas or Lunar New Year. The only npm package with holiday calendars, date-holidays, exposes a class you must construct, which this contract cannot call, so holidays belong in a lookup table the customer maintains and the caller adds the days itself. Say that in the first sentence of the docs or the name will mislead. Its weekend is also fixed at Saturday and Sunday, so a Friday–Saturday jurisdiction is not served at all. There is no working-hours clock either: '8 working hours from 4pm Friday' must be composed in the caller's flow. Verified under Node 20 CJS: addBusinessDays('2026-09-11', 5) = 2026-09-18, and date-fns v4 accepts an ISO string directly, so no separate parse step is needed.

functions.name: Add Business Days
functions.description: The due date N working days out, skipping weekends. Add public holidays from your own calendar table.

functions.name: Business Days Between
functions.description: Working days elapsed — the number an SLA report and a breach calculation are both built on.

functions.name: Is Weekend
functions.description: Whether a date falls on Saturday or Sunday, for a flow that must defer to the next working day.

functions.name: Add Days
functions.description: Calendar days, for a statutory clock that runs through weekends — a 28-day appeal window.

functions.name: Add Months
functions.description: Months added, clamped correctly at month end: 31 January plus one month is 28 or 29 February.

functions.name: Add Years
functions.description: The retention calculation — retain until seven years after closure, leap years handled.

functions.name: Calendar Days Between
functions.description: Whole calendar days, counting date boundaries rather than 24-hour periods, so a report is not off by one because of the time of day.

functions.name: Minutes Between
functions.description: Minutes between two timestamps — the raw elapsed figure an SLA subtracts paused time from.

functions.name: Is Past Due
functions.description: Whether one timestamp is after another; with now and the due date, this is the breach test.

catalogue.name: Money & Tax
catalogue.tagline: Exact decimal money arithmetic on strings — no floating point, no half-cent surprises.
catalogue.why: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, and in an invoicing, claims, grants or procurement app that becomes a one-cent variance an accountant will not sign off. Every function here works on two-decimal strings, so the amount that goes into the database is the amount that came out of the arithmetic. Percent Of applies GST/VAT/levy with half-up rounding at the cent — the rule most tax authorities state — with the rate supplied by the caller, so a rate change is a data change and not a release.
catalogue.risk: money-math is fixed at TWO decimal places: JPY and KRW (0 dp) and BHD, KWD, JOD, TND (3 dp) are simply wrong, so a multi-currency deployment must check Currency Info's digits before trusting it. Verified trap worth putting on the action itself: mul('19.99','3') returns 0.60, because '3' is read as 0.03 — both operands must be two-decimal strings, which is why Amount From Number is in this list. Rounding is half-up everywhere, so a jurisdiction requiring banker's rounding is not served. The package is small, dependency-free and stable but was last published years ago and its @types are community-maintained; the popular alternatives are all unusable here because their APIs chain (big.js, currency.js, decimal.js) or need currency objects (dinero.js, which is also ESM-only), and this contract permits exactly one call per action. Tax RATES and rules — thresholds, reverse charge, place of supply — are deliberately absent: they belong in the app's lookup tables. Verified: add('10.00','2.50')='12.50', percent('119.99','9.00')='10.80', format('USD','1234.50')='1,234.50' (grouping, no symbol).

functions.name: Add Amounts
functions.description: Exact addition of two two-decimal amount strings.

functions.name: Subtract Amounts
functions.description: Exact subtraction.

functions.name: Multiply Amount
functions.description: Amount times a quantity or rate. Both operands must be two-decimal strings — pass 3.00 for three, never 3.

functions.name: Divide Amount
functions.description: Amount divided by a two-decimal divisor, rounded half-up at the cent. Check the remainder separately when a split must be exact.

functions.name: Percent Of
functions.description: GST, VAT or a levy — a percentage of an amount, exactly, with the rate supplied as data.

functions.name: Compare Amounts
functions.description: Ordering for approval thresholds and reconciliation: negative, zero or positive.

functions.name: Amount From Number
functions.description: A number from a form becomes a safe two-decimal amount string — 3 becomes 3.00.

functions.name: Amount To Cents
functions.description: Minor units, for a payment gateway that wants integers.

functions.name: Format Amount
functions.description: Group an amount by the currency's convention, for an invoice line or a statement.

functions.name: Currency Info
functions.description: The ISO 4217 record — numeric code, minor-unit digits, name, countries. Check digits before trusting two-decimal arithmetic for that currency.
functions.returns: object { code, number, digits, currency, countries }

catalogue.name: Empty, Loading & Error States
catalogue.tagline: The three screens a data page spends most of its life in, made deliberate instead of blank.
catalogue.why: A list page is empty before its query returns, empty again when a filter matches nothing, and broken when a service is down — and by default all three render as nothing at all, which every user reads as a bug. This is those states with the right words, one action each, and a skeleton shaped like the content that is coming so the page does not jump when data lands.
catalogue.risk: This overlaps the built-in shadcn pack, which already has empty, skeleton and spinner, so the honest justification is shape rather than novelty: flat-prop components a designer binds in one gesture, plus the three states the built-ins have no answer for — NoResults, a table-shaped skeleton and PermissionDenied. If the built-in Empty grows props, half of this should be deleted rather than maintained beside it. The second risk is illustration: inline SVG is exactly where 'genuinely good, not placeholder-grade' is hardest with simple shapes, and a weak illustration is worse than none, so the default is an icon in a soft circle and the illustration is opt-in.

components.name: EmptyState
components.description: Nothing here yet — with the one action that changes that.
components.notes: A centred icon in a soft circle (color-mix over the muted token), title, one line, one primary action. The optional illustration is inline SVG in border and muted tones, never an image asset, so it themes instead of being a light-mode PNG on a dark page.

components.name: NoResults
components.description: The filtered-empty state, which is a different message from the empty one.
components.notes: Separate from EmptyState on purpose: 'no cases yet' invites creating one, 'no cases match' invites clearing the filter, and conflating them is how users get stuck on a screen they filtered themselves into. Clear filters is the primary action.

components.name: ErrorState
components.description: Something failed, in language a user can act on, with the id the service desk will ask for.
components.notes: A destructive-toned lucide AlertTriangle, a plain-language message, Retry, and a copyable correlation id — the reason to render this rather than a toast. technicalDetails hides the stack behind a native details/summary.

components.name: PermissionDenied
components.description: The 403 as a screen, naming the role required.
components.notes: A lucide Lock and a way to ask. Deliberately says nothing about whether the record exists, since confirming existence to someone who may not read it is itself a disclosure.

components.name: SkeletonTable
components.description: A placeholder shaped like the table that is loading.
components.notes: Matches the real table's column count and width ratios so the page does not jump when data arrives — the entire reason to prefer a skeleton over a spinner. Row width variation is a deterministic pattern, never Math.random, so it does not shimmer differently on every render.

components.name: LoadingOverlay
components.description: A refresh over content that is already there — not a first load.
components.notes: An absolute scrim over existing content. delayMs suppresses it below ~200ms so a fast query produces no flash — the detail that separates a considered loading state from an irritating one.

catalogue.name: Identifiers & Contact Data
catalogue.tagline: Check-digit validation and normalisation for national ids, tax numbers, IBANs, postcodes, phones and emails.
catalogue.why: A registry, a claims system or a procurement portal is mostly a pile of identifiers, and the same three bugs recur: the same person stored twice because one record has +65 91234567 and the other 9123 4567; a payment bounced on a mistyped IBAN nobody check-summed; an intake form that accepts a national id with a wrong check digit and fails three weeks later at the department that consumes it. Client-side validation is not validation — these are the server-side answers, one call each, with the country as a parameter so one flow serves several jurisdictions.
catalogue.risk: Coverage is per-locale and uneven, and that is the honest limit. isIdentityCard covers 15 locales (ES, FI, IN, IR, IT, LK, NO, PL, TH, he-IL, ar-LY, ar-TN, zh-CN, zh-HK, zh-TW) and does NOT cover Singapore NRIC/FIN or UEN, UK NINO or Malaysian MyKad — which is the first thing this audience will ask for, and the honest answer is a small code component with the check-digit loop, since one CallFunction cannot express one. isTaxID covers 36 mostly-EU locales, isPostalCode 70. An unsupported locale THROWS rather than returning false, so every call needs an exception handler in the flow — a real trap. Everything here checks FORMAT and CHECK DIGITS only: whether an identifier belongs to a live person or company needs a registry feed no package supplies. libphonenumber's metadata is a point-in-time snapshot of numbering plans and goes stale between pins, and its full metadata is ~150 kB inherited by every consumer (irrelevant on Node, but it is inherited). validator's isVAT did not validate genuine GB numbers in testing and is deliberately excluded. Verified under CJS: isPostalCode('018956','SG')=true, formatNumber({country:'SG',phone:'91234567'},'E.164')='+6591234567', isValidIBAN('DE89370400440532013000')=true.

functions.name: Is Email
functions.description: Whether a string is a deliverable-shaped email address.

functions.name: Normalise Email
functions.description: Canonical form for de-duplicating accounts — lower-cases the domain and applies provider rules, so A.B+ref@Gmail.com and ab@gmail.com match as one subject.

functions.name: Check Phone Number
functions.description: A real, dialable number for that country — the numbering plan, not a regex.

functions.name: Normalise Phone Number
functions.description: A locally-typed number to E.164 for storage, so the same person is never stored twice.

functions.name: Check Postal Code
functions.description: Country-specific postcode check across 70 locales, or 'any'.

functions.name: Check National Id
functions.description: A national identity number against its country's format and check digit — Aadhaar's Verhoeff, the Spanish DNI letter, the Italian codice fiscale. Throws on an unsupported locale, so branch on country first.

functions.name: Check Tax Id
functions.description: A tax identification number for 36 locales, including US SSN/ITIN (en-US) and most EU national schemes.

functions.name: Check IBAN
functions.description: Country length, structure and the mod-97 check. Call it before a payment run, not after the rejection.

functions.name: Normalise IBAN
functions.description: Strip spaces and upper-case into the electronic form, which is what to store and compare on.

functions.name: Check BIC
functions.description: SWIFT/BIC structure and country segment, for the other half of a payment instruction.

catalogue.name: Text, Names & Matching
catalogue.tagline: Case conversion, slugs, transliteration and the fuzzy match that maps an imported name onto a record you hold.
catalogue.why: Two string chores nobody plans for. The first is shape: a case title into a URL slug, a field name into a column header, a CJK or accented supplier name into a Latin search key. The second is the hard part of every import — the file says 'Ministry of Health (HQ)' and your table says 'Ministry of Health'. Every team writes that fuzzy match by hand and gets it wrong; here it is two calls used together.
catalogue.risk: Closest Match always returns something: given 400 supplier names it hands back the least-wrong one for an input that matches nothing, so used alone it silently writes bad references into a database. It must be paired with Edit Distance and a threshold the caller chooses, and a one-call-per-action library cannot enforce that discipline — the right shape would be one action returning { match, distance } and there is no upstream export for it. Levenshtein is character distance, so 'Health, Ministry of' scores worse than a plain typo; token-based matching (Jaro-Winkler, trigram) suits reconciliation better and no pure-function CommonJS package offers it in one call. change-case is frozen at 4.1.2 because 5.x is ESM-only, so that pin can never move. Every popular slug package is default-export-only or ESM; transliteration is used because it genuinely exposes a named slugify and also handles CJK and Cyrillic, which a multilingual registry needs. Verified: slugify('Ministère de Santé')='ministere-de-sante', transliterate('北京')='Bei Jing', distance('Acme Pte Ltd','Acme Pte. Ltd')=1.

functions.name: To Camel Case
functions.description: "case status" → "caseStatus", for an API payload key.

functions.name: To Capital Case
functions.description: "case_status" → "Case Status", for a column header derived from a field name.

functions.name: To Kebab Case
functions.description: "Case Status" → "case-status", for routes and ids.

functions.name: To Snake Case
functions.description: "caseStatus" → "case_status", for a legacy database or a CSV header a partner specified.

functions.name: To Sentence Case
functions.description: "caseStatus" → "Case status", for a generated label.

functions.name: Slugify
functions.description: Any title — accented, Cyrillic or CJK — to a URL-safe slug.

functions.name: Transliterate
functions.description: Non-Latin names to Latin script, for search keys and printed forms.

functions.name: Edit Distance
functions.description: How many single-character edits separate two strings. Zero is exact; 2-3 catches typos without inventing matches.

functions.name: Closest Match
functions.description: The nearest candidate in a list — an imported department or supplier mapped onto the value you already hold. Always pair it with Edit Distance and refuse a match above your threshold.

catalogue.name: Masked & Formatted Fields
catalogue.tagline: Currency, percent, phone and identifier inputs that format as you type and emit clean values.
catalogue.why: Line-of-business forms capture money, rates, phone numbers, identifiers and reporting periods. Without masks a user types '1,250.00' into a Decimal field and the action stores a string, or types a national id without separators and validation fires after submit. These format on the way in, hand the action a clean number or a digits-only string, and share one label/hint/error frame so a form looks like one form.
catalogue.risk: Caret management in a controlled masked input is the classic bug source: every reformat must restore selectionStart in a useLayoutEffect, and paste, IME composition, Android soft keyboards and Backspace over a mask literal each need their own case. The platform sharpens it — coerceParam turns an empty Decimal binding into 0, so 'empty' and 'zero' are indistinguishable unless the component keeps a private draft string, which means it holds state about a value the page also owns and can desynchronise on an external write. Checksum rules go stale, so IdentifierInput offers generic Luhn and mod-11 rather than naming a national scheme it cannot keep current. MonthPicker and TimePicker exist because the built-in shadcn calendar is a date input and has neither; DatePicker deliberately is NOT here, since reimplementing react-day-picker's keyboard and locale handling would be a regression.

components.name: FieldFrame
components.description: The shared label / required marker / hint / error frame the other fields sit in.
components.notes: Imported by the others as @/components/FieldFrame — the local specifier the contract allows for a sibling of the same library — so label and error styling exist once.

components.name: CurrencyInput
components.description: Grouped, symbol-prefixed money entry that emits a number, not a formatted string.
components.notes: Intl.NumberFormat, a browser built-in, so no money library in the browser. Formats on blur and keeps raw digits editable while focused, which is what stops the caret jumping mid-entry.

components.name: PercentInput
components.description: Percentage entry that states whether it stores 15 or 0.15.
components.notes: The fraction-versus-percent trap is a declared prop rather than a guess, because the same rate is stored both ways across two tables in most real schemas.

components.name: NumberStepper
components.description: Bounded quantity input with minus/plus and a unit suffix.
components.notes: lucide Minus and Plus; hold-to-repeat is a setInterval started on pointerdown and cleared on pointerup AND pointercancel, so a finger lifted outside the button still stops it.

components.name: PhoneInput
components.description: Pattern-masked phone entry showing '+65 9123-4567' and emitting digits only.
components.notes: A literal mask where # is a digit — deliberately not libphonenumber, which is not an allowed browser import; real validation belongs in the identifier library on the server. Country rules are app data: pass a pattern per country from a lookup table.

components.name: IdentifierInput
components.description: Masked registry identifiers with an optional checksum — case, policy, licence and account numbers.
components.notes: Luhn and mod-11 are about ten lines each, written inline, and are generic algorithms — the component never claims to validate a jurisdiction it cannot keep current.

components.name: MonthPicker
components.description: Reporting-period picker: a 3×4 month grid with a year pager, no day grid at all.
components.notes: Deliberately not a calendar with the days hidden — a period is a different thing from a date, and this is twelve buttons and two chevrons.

components.name: TimePicker
components.description: Hour and minute columns in a popover, stepped and bounded.
components.notes: Two scrollable columns of buttons rather than <input type="time">, whose rendering and keyboard behaviour differ per browser and cannot be styled to match the rest of the form.

components.name: WorkingDaysHint
components.description: 'Target: 14 Mar (10 working days)' under a date field, counting forward past weekends and given holidays.
components.notes: A loop over [y, m, d] integers — integers inside, ISO at the edges, which is the discipline that keeps a picker from showing the wrong day west of Greenwich. The holiday list is app data, usually a lookup table, and weekendDays covers Fri/Sat regions the server library cannot.

catalogue.name: Audit Trail & Change Tracking
catalogue.tagline: What changed field by field, canonical bytes that hash the same in five years, and time-ordered audit ids.
catalogue.why: 'Show me the audit trail' is the first thing an auditor asks and the last thing an app is built for. Two questions have to be answerable: who changed what, from what value to what — normally a per-entity comparison loop that goes stale the day someone adds an attribute — and whether a row was edited afterwards, which a timestamp column proves nothing about. Canonical Record is RFC 8785 JCS, so the same record always serialises to the same bytes; Record Digest chains an entry to its predecessor; Audit Id is a ULID, so an append-only table sorts in creation order as plain text without trusting a clock column.
catalogue.risk: This is a hash chain, not notarisation: anyone who can rewrite the whole table can recompute every digest, so the tamper evidence only holds if the head digest is periodically published somewhere the app cannot write — a nightly mail to the auditor, a second store, a regulator's receipt. That step is a deployment decision the library cannot make. There is no keyed HMAC (js-sha256's hmac hangs off sha256.hmac and is not a named export), so an insider with write access and the code can forge a chain. The chaining itself is a concatenation the CALLER performs in an Assign, because one CallFunction is one call, and verifying a whole chain is a loop in the caller's flow. And the diff is structural JSON while a Prisma row is not: updatedAt differs on every save, Decimal and Date compare by shape, relations arrive nested — hand it a whole row and it reports noise on every write, so the caller MUST project the fields it cares about first (the PII library's Pick Fields, or a Query projection). Verified: detailedDiff returns {added, deleted, updated}; canonicalize({b:2,a:1})='{"a":1,"b":2}'; and ulid exports NO isValid, so an id-format check must be a length-and-charset rule in the flow.

functions.name: Field Changes
functions.description: The three-way detail between two versions of a record — added, deleted, updated — as one audit row built from data rather than a hand-written comparison.

functions.name: Changed Values
functions.description: Only the fields whose value actually changed, flat. The short form for a timeline entry or a change-request summary.

functions.name: Canonical Record
functions.description: RFC 8785 canonical JSON — keys sorted, numbers and unicode in one fixed form — so a digest taken today still matches in five years.

functions.name: Record Digest
functions.description: SHA-256 as lower-case hex. Feed it the canonical record, or the previous digest concatenated with it, to chain an entry to its predecessor.

functions.name: Audit Id
functions.description: A ULID: 26 characters whose leading bits are the timestamp, so ids sort in creation order as plain text — the primary key for an append-only table nobody can reconcile across services otherwise.

functions.name: Audit Id Time
functions.description: The creation time recovered from a ULID, so an entry's own id proves when it was written without trusting a separate column.

catalogue.name: Timelines, Audit Trails & People
catalogue.tagline: Who did what, when — activity feeds, approval chains and audit trails, with the people attached.
catalogue.why: Audit history is a statutory requirement in most of these apps and is always rebuilt from scratch: audit rows turned into readable prose, grouped by day, with the actor's initials and a relative time that says '4 hours ago' without a date library. This is that, plus the approval chain a reviewer scrolls to before deciding — the two read-only surfaces on nearly every record page in case management.
catalogue.risk: Feeds are where someone else's data model shows through: these take generic key props because the row shape belongs to the developer, which means the component cannot make the sentence read naturally — 'Sagar changed Status from Draft to Submitted' needs a template, and a template prop is a small language nobody wants to learn; the children slot covers it but is awkward to bind in a low-code inspector. A long trail needs virtualisation to stay usable past a few thousand rows and no virtualisation library is on the allow-list, so paging is the only honest answer. The deterministic avatar hue borrows the chart ramp for identity, so a page carrying both a chart and an avatar group has two meanings for the same five colours — defensible, but decide it deliberately.

components.name: ActivityFeed
components.description: A stream of events on a record, grouped by day with sticky headings.
components.notes: The rail is one absolutely-positioned 1px div behind the items, with each icon dot in bg-card so the rail appears to break at the dot rather than run underneath it — the detail that separates a timeline from a bulleted list. Day grouping compares Intl.DateTimeFormat parts in the supplied timeZone, never local midnight, so a burst of events does not split at the wrong hour for a reader in another region.

components.name: TimelineItem
components.description: One event on the rail, usable alone inside a detail panel.
components.notes: Composes @/components/InitialsAvatar and @/components/RelativeTime so an item, a feed and an audit row render a person and a time identically. The children slot takes something richer — a comment, an attachment row, a field diff.

components.name: ApprovalChain
components.description: The decision path — who approved, who rejected, and where it stopped.
components.notes: Avatar, name, outcome badge and time joined by a 2px rail that turns primary once passed and destructive at a rejection, so the point of failure is findable without reading. Pending steps are dashed and muted — the one place a dashed line earns itself, because it means 'not yet'.

components.name: AuditTrail
components.description: The compliance view of the same events: actor, action, field, before, after, stamp.
components.notes: Tabular, with tabular-nums on the timestamp column so stamps align down the page and an explicit zone suffix on every one — the thing an auditor asks for first. Field changes render through the record library's FieldDiffRow where present, so 'what changed' is not drawn two ways in one app.

components.name: RelativeTime
components.description: '4 hours ago', with the exact stamp one hover away.
components.notes: Intl.RelativeTimeFormat for the phrase, Intl.DateTimeFormat for the title attribute — no date library, localisation free. Renders a <time dateTime> and an em-dash for an unparseable value rather than 'Invalid Date'. The tooltip always carries the absolute time with its zone, because a relative time alone is not an audit record.

components.name: InitialsAvatar
components.description: A person as initials or a photo, the same colour on every screen.
components.notes: A small string hash mod 5 onto chart-1..chart-5, so one person keeps one colour across the app. Falls back to initials when the image 404s (an onError swap, the case hand-rolled avatars always forget) and to a lucide User when the name is empty. Identity colour only — it never reaches for the status tones.

components.name: AvatarGroup
components.description: Assignees or watchers, overlapped, with an overflow chip.
components.notes: -space-x-2 with a 2px ring in the card colour — the ring, not a border, is what separates them cleanly against any surface. The overflow chip carries the remaining names in its title.

catalogue.name: Approval & Case Actions
catalogue.tagline: The decision bar, the reasoned dialog, the four-eyes panel and the case comment thread.
catalogue.why: Every approval app rebuilds the same surfaces on its task page: a decision bar, a confirm dialog that will not close until a reason is typed, a sign-off panel showing which of three roles have signed, a comment thread with internal notes, and a bulk bar over a selected list. They are the difference between a workflow that runs and one an officer can work in, and none of them is in the widget vocabulary today.
catalogue.risk: These sit next to the platform's own TaskInbox widget and the workflow engine's Approval and HumanTask nodes, so there is a real duplication question: if a component decides what 'approve' means it will drift from the workflow definition. The library is only defensible while it stays strictly presentational and the decision keys come from the model — it reports, it never applies. canDecide is a HINT the page wires from session.hasRole(...), and a careless integrator gets a sign-off button that looks authoritative while the server enforces nothing, which is worse than no button at all. CommentThread takes an unbounded array with no virtualisation available, so collapsedCount is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.

components.name: DecisionBar
components.description: The sticky decision bar on a task page: due date, assignee, and the decisions available.
components.notes: One primary button and the rest outline, so a page never shows two competing primaries — the platform's one-primary-action rule expressed as a component rather than left to a review. tone maps through a three-entry static table of full class strings, never an interpolated class name.

components.name: DecisionDialog
components.description: Confirm with a mandatory reason: canned reasons, a minimum length, no dismiss-by-clicking-away.
components.notes: @radix-ui/react-alert-dialog, so it is modal and focus-trapped. Confirm stays disabled until the reason clears reasonMinLength — the control auditors ask about, expressed once instead of per page.

components.name: SignOffPanel
components.description: Four-eyes approval: which roles must sign, who already has, with what comment, and whether the viewer may still decide.
components.notes: Approve is the single primary action; Reject is a quiet outline button, so the panel presents one visual decision rather than two competing ones.

components.name: CommentThread
components.description: Case correspondence: public replies and internal notes, with attachments and relative times.
components.notes: Internal notes take a distinct left border and a bg-muted ground so nobody mails an internal note to an applicant. Posting emits an event; the component never makes a request.

components.name: AssigneePicker
components.description: Reassign or delegate, showing each candidate's current workload.
components.notes: Radix Popover with initials, name, role and a small load bar, so a supervisor sees who is free without opening a report.

components.name: BulkActionBar
components.description: Appears when rows are selected: the count, the bulk actions, and clear.
components.notes: Renders null at zero so the page needs no If wrapper. It emits only — confirmation is DecisionDialog's job, which keeps reason capture in one place.

catalogue.name: CSV & Delimited Files
catalogue.tagline: Read and write CSV, TSV and pipe-delimited files the way partners actually send them.
catalogue.why: Every registry, claims and procurement app has an import screen and an export button, and CSV is what finance, HR, banks and government partners send — not xlsx. Without this a developer writes split(",") and then meets quoted commas, embedded newlines, CRLF, ragged rows and a semicolon-delimited file from a European ERP in production. This is the missing half of the built-in Excel nodes: the same import screen has to accept both.
catalogue.risk: parse returns a wrapper { data, errors, meta }, not rows, and a one-call body cannot unwrap it — every caller writes {{result.data}} and one who forgets gets an object where they expected an array. In the other direction, unparse produces a STRING and a library cannot write an AppFile, so 'download this as CSV' still needs a server action returning the text or a REST response: this makes the bytes, not the file, and that gap is the first thing anyone will ask about. No BOM can be prepended inside a single call, so Excel on a European desktop will mangle accented names in an exported file. Parsing is fully in memory (papaparse's streaming API is callback-based and unusable through CallFunction), so a 200 MB extract is out of scope. Interop is the safe part: papaparse 5.4.1 is UMD CommonJS with real named exports and @types that declare them — verified parsing a header row with dynamic typing and requiring unparse.

functions.name: Parse CSV
functions.description: Parse a CSV string into objects keyed by the header row. Read {{result.data}} for the rows and {{result.errors}} to tell the person which lines were ragged.

functions.name: Parse Delimited Text
functions.description: The same for a file that is not comma-separated — semicolon from a European export, tab, or pipe.

functions.name: Parse CSV Rows
functions.description: Parse a headerless file into arrays of cells, for fixed-position extracts from a mainframe or a bank.

functions.name: Detect Delimiter
functions.description: Read the first line only and report the delimiter that was inferred, so an import screen can say what it thinks the file is before parsing all of it.

functions.name: Build CSV
functions.description: An array of objects to a CSV string, header row taken from the first object's keys.

functions.name: Build CSV With Columns
functions.description: Exactly these columns, in exactly this order, whatever else the rows carry — the export an interface agreement specifies.

functions.name: Build Delimited Text
functions.description: Write with a chosen delimiter and line ending, for a partner whose spec says semicolon and CRLF.

catalogue.name: Pickers, Tags & Lookups
catalogue.tagline: Searchable pickers whose results come from your own action instead of a fetch.
catalogue.why: Back-office forms are full of 'pick the vendor', 'tag this case', 'choose the officers to notify'. A plain Select cannot search, and the built-in Command palette is a keyboard surface rather than a record picker with a subtitle line and a workload column. Each of these is driven by an onSearch event, so the module's own Query action supplies the rows and the component never touches the network.
catalogue.risk: Real overlap with what already ships — the built-in shadcn pack has command, select and popover — so the justification has to be the business affordances (server-driven results, two-line record rows, emitting id and label together) and not the widget existing. Accessibility is the hard part and nothing type-checks it: a hand-rolled listbox that omits aria-activedescendant and roving focus is a regression in exactly the public-sector settings this targets. Debouncing inside the component also fights the platform: the thing being debounced is the page's action, and a slow response can land after a newer one with no request id to discard it, so a stale result can overwrite a fresh one — the page must guard that, and nothing reminds it to.

components.name: Combobox
components.description: Single-select with a search box, loading state and an empty state.
components.notes: Radix Popover plus a filtered <ul> — no cmdk. Filtering is local String.includes when onSearch is unbound and server-driven when it is bound (the page action refills options). The component never fetches; it only reports the query.

components.name: MultiCombobox
components.description: Multi-select with checkbox rows and an 'n selected' summary on the closed trigger.
components.notes: @radix-ui/react-checkbox rows so the checked state is accessible; sticky group headers inside a max-h-72 scroll area. Past maxVisible the trigger reads '4 departments' rather than growing without bound.

components.name: RecordLookup
components.description: A record picker with two-line results — a subtitle and a meta column — for vendors, cases or officers.
components.notes: Debounce is a setTimeout in a useEffect with a cleanup — no lodash. It emits both the id and the label, so the page stores a foreign key and still shows a name after reload without a second read.

components.name: TagInput
components.description: Free-text chips with optional suggestions, a max count and duplicate rejection.
components.notes: Enter and comma commit, Backspace on an empty field removes the last chip. Suggestions render in a Radix Popover as a role=listbox with a roving arrow-key index.

components.name: HierarchySelect
components.description: Pick from a tree — org units, categories, account codes — flattened from parentId.
components.notes: Depth becomes indentation through a six-entry static class map (pl-0 … pl-20), because pl-${depth*4} would not compile. Expansion is a useState<Set<string>>.

components.name: TokenTextArea
components.description: A textarea with an insert-token menu, for notification and letter templates.
components.notes: A plain textarea plus a Radix dropdown; inserting splices {{token}} at selectionStart and restores the caret after it in a useLayoutEffect. Pairs with the Merge Fields functions that render the result.

catalogue.name: Metrics & KPI Tiles
catalogue.tagline: The KPI row every console opens with — stat tiles, deltas, sparklines, rings and proportional bars.
catalogue.why: Every service desk, claims console and procurement dashboard opens with a row of numbers: open cases, overdue, this week against last. Without this a developer hand-builds a Box+Text stack per tile, formats the number by hand, and ships no trend at all — or reaches for a charting package that is not on the allow-list. This removes the dashboard header as a build task and makes the most-looked-at element of the app consistent between screens.
catalogue.risk: Deliberately stops short of a chart library: the forms here are the ones that need no axis, no tick selection and no measurement — a polyline in a stretched viewBox, a dash-offset ring, a flex-grow strip. A full BarChart/LineChart set was considered and dropped, because the cheap parts are not the hard parts (nice ticks on ugly ranges, label collision, negative values, irregular time axes) and it quietly becomes an unmaintained chart library with a bug queue; anything needing axes should stay a table or a server-rendered image until that is a deliberate project. Number formatting is the remaining deep end: Intl covers compact, currency and percent, but durations ('2d 4h') and a sensible precision policy are hand-written and wrong is visible on the element people look at first. The sparkline's degenerate case — every value equal — collapses onto the baseline and reads as 'no data' unless special-cased.

components.name: StatTile
components.description: One headline metric with an optional delta, icon and inline trend — the unit a KPI row is made of.
components.notes: Type and spacing, no SVG in the tile itself. Value through Intl.NumberFormat (notation compact for 12.9K). Delta tone is direction × deltaGoodWhen rather than the sign, because a falling backlog is good news, and it carries a lucide arrow so it is never colour-alone.

components.name: StatTileGroup
components.description: The responsive band that holds a row of tiles and keeps them reading as one object.
components.notes: CSS grid stepping from one column at phone width. When divided, tiles share a 1px border-border rule instead of gaps, so the row reads as a console header rather than a pile of floating cards.

components.name: Sparkline
components.description: A 12-to-60 point trend line sized to whatever column it lands in.
components.notes: A <polyline> in a fixed viewBox '0 0 100 32' with preserveAspectRatio=none, so it stretches to any width with no ResizeObserver. vector-effect=non-scaling-stroke keeps the line 2px under that non-uniform scale — the trap that makes most hand-rolled sparklines look smeared. Colour is stroke=currentColor under a text-* class.

components.name: DeltaBadge
components.description: A signed change chip whose colour means good or bad, not up or down.
components.notes: Soft background as color-mix(in oklab, currentColor 12%, transparent), so one class controls ink and fill and dark mode needs no dark: variant.

components.name: ProgressRing
components.description: A circular percentage — SLA consumed, budget drawn down, completion.
components.notes: Two concentric circles, strokeDasharray 2πr and strokeDashoffset 2πr·(1−value/max), rotated −90° so it starts at twelve o'clock. strokeLinecap round is dropped below ~2% or the cap alone renders as a full dot at zero. The centred value is HTML over the SVG, never <text>, which ignores the app's type scale and clips at small sizes.

components.name: Meter
components.description: A linear gauge with severity thresholds, for capacity and utilisation.
components.notes: A div track with a width-% fill, no SVG. The unfilled track is a lighter step of the same ramp rather than a grey, so the state reads across the whole bar. Threshold marks are 1px absolutely-positioned rules.

components.name: ComparisonBar
components.description: Actual against target in the space of one line — the bullet chart.
components.notes: Three plain divs: a muted range band, an 8px actual bar, a 2px full-height target tick. No axis and no gridlines — the two labels carry the numbers, which is the point of the form.

components.name: StackedBarStrip
components.description: A queue's composition as one proportional band — 32 open, 8 overdue, 4 on hold.
components.notes: A flex row of divs with flex-grow per value and gap-[2px], rounded on the outer ends only. Flexbox does the proportional arithmetic, so it reflows at any width with zero measurement — the cheapest correct chart there is, and usually the right answer when someone asked for a pie.

catalogue.name: Markdown, Merge Fields & Safe HTML
catalogue.tagline: Render markdown, sanitise it, fill a letter's merge fields, and write an amount in words.
catalogue.why: Business apps are full of authored text that is not an email: case notes and knowledge articles stored as markdown and shown on a page, a decision letter whose wording is a template with {{applicantName}} in it, a PDF body composed before the built-in PdfExport node draws it, a payment voucher that must carry the amount in words. The built-in EmailTemplate covers email and only email, deliberately; everything else is currently string concatenation inside expressions, which is where escaping bugs live.
catalogue.risk: The sanitiser was the thing most likely to make this unbuildable, so I checked it rather than assumed: sanitize-html is `export = sanitizeHtml` and unreachable by a generator that emits a named import, but `xss` genuinely exposes filterXSS as a named export and requires cleanly under Node 20 CJS — verified, and it stripped an onerror attribute from an while keeping the markup around it. The cost is that its allow-list is a per-call options object passed as a {{= }} expression, so a default-deny policy has to be written by whoever wires it, and a caller who renders markdown from a public form without calling Sanitize HTML has stored XSS — pair it in the docs and in the RichTextView notes. marked's CommonJS story moved across majors, so 12.0.2 is a deliberate pin and an upgrade is a compatibility check rather than a bump. mustache escapes {{ }} by default, which is right for HTML and wrong for plain text and file names, hence a separate action passing an identity escape — a subtlety that will be got wrong at least once. Amount In Words is English only, which rules out a bilingual voucher.

functions.name: Render Markdown
functions.description: Markdown to HTML, GitHub-flavoured, single newlines kept as line breaks — what people expect when they type into a notes box.

functions.name: Render Markdown Inline
functions.description: The same with no surrounding block element, for a one-line notice, a table cell or a heading that carries emphasis.

functions.name: Sanitize HTML
functions.description: Strip scripts, event handlers and javascript: links from HTML before it is stored or rendered. Call it on anything that did not come from your own staff.

functions.name: Escape HTML
functions.description: Escape a value from outside before it is placed in HTML you are assembling — a partner's product name, a field from an uploaded row.

functions.name: Decode HTML Entities
functions.description: Turn é and é back into é. Legacy CSV and XML feeds are full of double-encoded entities and this is the fix.

functions.name: Merge Fields Into HTML
functions.description: Fill {{placeholders}} in a template from an object, escaping every substituted value. The template is authored by staff; the values are data.

functions.name: Merge Fields Into Text
functions.description: The same for plain text — a PDF body, an SMS, a file name, a reference pattern — with escaping off so an ampersand stays an ampersand.

functions.name: Amount In Words
functions.description: 1234 → "one thousand, two hundred thirty-four", for a cheque, a voucher or a deed.

catalogue.name: Wizards & Data Import
catalogue.tagline: Multi-step intake and the five screens every import needs: drop, map, check, run, review.
catalogue.why: Every application form, licence renewal and onboarding flow is the same shape — a step tracker, a framed body, a sticky Back/Next footer, a 'check your answers' screen — and every line-of-business app eventually grows an import wizard on top of it. The column mapper alone (target field on the left, a select of the file's headers on the right, a sample value underneath, required-but-unmapped flagged) is a day of work repeated per app and never quite consistent, and the part everyone skips is showing the errors before anything is written.
catalogue.risk: These are chrome: the wizard's state machine still lives in page variables and client actions, so a developer wires currentKey and several events per page — if that wiring is the real cost, this moves work rather than removing it, and the honest alternative is an Etyma-native wizard page template. WizardFrame depends on the children slot, which is the least-exercised path in the page designer. FileDropzone reads the whole file into browser memory and hands it to an action as a string; roughly 5 MB of base64 in a JSON action call is the practical ceiling and business users do send 50 MB spreadsheets — the component can report that failure but cannot fix it, and the real answer is a direct-to-storage upload route, which is platform work. ValidationPreview re-renders its whole table on every issue change with no virtualisation available, so paging is the mitigation and a 5,000-row file will feel slow. Every error cell needs aria-invalid and a text alternative, not a colour ring, or the library fails procurement.

components.name: StepTracker
components.description: The numbered step rail — done, current, upcoming, error — horizontal or vertical.
components.notes: Circles are divs, connectors are flex-1 rules of bg-border, the done mark is a lucide Check. State styling goes through a four-entry const map of full literal class strings — never bg-${state}, which Tailwind does not compile. Below sm it collapses to 'Step 2 of 4 — Map columns' and carries aria-current=step.

components.name: WizardFrame
components.description: Title, step caption, a slot for the step body, and the sticky action footer.
components.notes: acceptsChildren is on, so the page drops its real widgets into the slot and the model keeps owning the fields. One primary button (Next, or Submit when isLastStep); Back and Save draft are ghost buttons, so the footer never shows two competing primaries.

components.name: ReviewSummary
components.description: The final 'check your answers' screen: grouped label/value pairs with an Edit link per section.
components.notes: A definition-list grid collapsing to one column at sm. Nested items arrive as unknown inside Object[], so the component narrows with a small typed reader rather than casting — strict tsc runs on the export.

components.name: RequiredFieldsNotice
components.description: A validation summary that names what is missing and jumps back to the step that owns it.
components.notes: role=alert with a lucide TriangleAlert, bg-destructive/10 border-destructive/30 — token colours with an alpha modifier, which Tailwind resolves statically.

components.name: FileDropzone
components.description: A drop target and browse button that reads a chosen file and hands its contents to a bound action.
components.notes: Native drag events on a div plus a visually hidden <input type=file> — no react-dnd. FileReader per readAs, with the data-URL prefix stripped before sending. Focusable and Enter/Space-activated, so it is not mouse-only.

components.name: UploadList
components.description: Per-file rows with size, status, a progress track and retry.
props: files (Array<{id, name, size, status, progress?, error?}>)
components.notes: Icons from a static mime-prefix map so class strings stay literal; the progress track is an inner div with an inline style width, which is a value rather than a class name and therefore the safe way to express a computed size.

components.name: ColumnMapper
components.description: Maps the file's columns onto the fields your entity expects, with a sample value under each choice.
components.notes: Radix Select per target field with a 'Not imported' option and the first sample value beneath in text-xs. Auto-match lowercases and strips punctuation on both sides. Required-and-unmapped rows take a destructive ring and a lucide AlertCircle; unclaimed source columns are listed in a footer so nothing disappears silently.

components.name: ValidationPreview
components.description: The parsed rows as a table with failing cells marked and a count of what will be rejected — before anything is written.
components.notes: A hand-rolled table with a sticky header; a cell with an issue takes ring-1 ring-destructive plus aria-invalid and a title carrying the message. A summary bar reads '12 errors, 3 warnings in 400 rows' with a toggle to show only problem rows.

components.name: ImportSummary
components.description: The end-of-run panel: created, updated, skipped, rejected, with one way to get the rejected rows and one way to finish.
components.notes: Four figures in a responsive grid, the failed one destructive-toned only when non-zero, one primary Done button and a quiet link for the rejected-rows file.

catalogue.name: PII Masking & Redaction
catalogue.tagline: Mask a value, drop a field, or pseudonymise a subject before data reaches a log, an export or a screenshot.
catalogue.why: Every line-of-business app leaks PII sideways: into request logs, into a CSV a caseworker mails out, into an error report, into a support screenshot. Developers hand-roll a substring-and-asterisks helper per field, get the boundary wrong, and ship an audit finding. Mask Record covers a 40-column entity in one call; Pick Fields and Omit Fields are the projection step before a record is diffed, logged or sent; Pseudonym For gives a stable irreversible token so analytics and de-duplication survive removing the identifier itself.
catalogue.risk: maskdata masks by POSITION, not by meaning: it never finds PII inside free text, and free-text detection is a genuine gap here — redact-pii exposes a constructor, which this contract cannot call, so scanning a case note needs a model call or a component of its own. Pseudonym For is a plain SHA-256, not a keyed HMAC (js-sha256's hmac hangs off sha256.hmac and is not a named export), so the salt must be concatenated by the caller and a leaked salt makes a short identifier — a 9-digit number, a national id — brute-forceable in seconds. maskdata is a small single-maintainer package whose maskString is already deprecated in favour of maskStringV2. And this is a hygiene layer, not a control: it cannot stop a query that selected the column in the first place. Verified under CJS: maskEmail2, maskPhone, maskCard, maskStringV2, maskJSON2 and maskJwt all resolve as named exports and maskEmail2 masked a real address.

functions.name: Mask Phone Number
functions.description: Keep the trailing digits a caseworker uses to confirm identity over the counter.

functions.description: Mask a JWT or bearer token so a request trace can be kept without keeping the credential.
