catalogue.name: Evidence, Attachments & Attestation
catalogue.tagline: Files, signatures, photos, consent and the declaration block above Submit.
catalogue.why: Claims, inspections and licence applications end in evidence: the attached invoice, the signed declaration, the site photos, the three statements the applicant is attesting to, and the consent record an auditor will ask about. Each is normally a small pile of custom code with a canvas or a hidden file input, done slightly differently on every page — and the attachment list is on nearly every record screen in the product.
catalogue.risk: SignaturePad is the component most likely to fail on this platform specifically: it measures a canvas, and the page designer mounts components before layout settles — this repository already records 'a canvas measured before it had width' as a lost session — so without a ResizeObserver and a redraw-from-value path the stroke vanishes on every re-render the model triggers. Data URLs are the second cost: a full-width signature is 30-100 KB of base64 living in a page variable and travelling through an action input, so maxSizeMb has to be a low, documented ceiling with real uploads going through a server action and the platform's AppFile storage. DocumentPreviewDialog's iframe is blocked by strict CSP and by X-Frame-Options on a file route, so download must be the assumed path and preview the bonus. ConsentList records a decision but is not a lawful-basis engine: which consent is required, and whether consent is even the right basis, is a legal question the app answers.

components.name: AttachmentList
components.description: The files on a record: type icon, name, size, when it arrived, a download link and an optional remove.
props: files (Array<{id, name, mimeType, size, url, uploadedAt, uploadedBy?, digest?}>)
components.notes: A lucide icon per mime prefix in a rounded bg-muted square, the name truncating with min-w-0, size in tabular-nums. Remove is a two-step in-row confirm ('Remove?') rather than a dialog, so a mis-click costs nothing. The empty state is a line of muted text, never a blank box.

components.name: DocumentPreviewDialog
components.description: Opens a file in place — images inline, PDFs in a frame, everything else as a download — so a reviewer does not lose the page.
components.notes: @radix-ui/react-dialog at max-w-3xl. The download button is present in all three states, not just the fallback one, because the frame is assumed to fail somewhere.

components.name: SignaturePad
components.description: Draw-to-sign on a canvas with a declaration line and a clear button; emits a PNG data URL.
components.notes: Pointer events with quadratic smoothing, scaled by devicePixelRatio and re-measured through a ResizeObserver; touch-action:none so a finger stroke does not scroll the page. On re-render the stored value is drawn back through an Image, so a model write never blanks the pad.

components.name: PhotoGrid
components.description: Thumbnail grid for inspection photos, with a lightbox and per-tile remove.
components.notes: aspect-square object-cover tiles; the lightbox is a Radix Dialog so focus is trapped and Escape closes. Column count maps through a five-entry static table because grid-cols-${n} does not compile.

components.name: RatingScale
components.description: Stars, a 1-5 scale or a 0-10 NPS row, read-only or interactive.
components.notes: lucide Star with fill-current toggled per index — two literal class strings, never interpolated. NPS is eleven buttons that wrap below sm, with arrow-key support over a radiogroup role.

components.name: AttestationBox
components.description: The declaration block above Submit: statements to tick, a signer line, a gated confirm.
components.notes: @radix-ui/react-checkbox rows in a bordered card; the confirm button stays disabled until requireAll is satisfied, which is the rule an auditor actually asks about.

components.name: ConsentList
components.description: The purposes a subject has or has not consented to, with when and how each was captured.
props: purposes (Array<{id, label, description, required, granted, grantedAt, source}>)
components.notes: Required rows are disabled and marked rather than hidden. grantedAt and source render as a text-xs muted line under the label — the record an auditor asks for, not just the current state.

catalogue.name: XML, YAML & Schema Validation
catalogue.tagline: Read the formats partners hand over, and refuse a bad payload at the door.
catalogue.why: Public-sector and financial integrations are XML long after everything else moved on — UBL invoices, PEPPOL, ISO 20022, statutory returns — and Etyma can fetch such a document today but cannot read it, so the only route is a regex in an expression, which is how a production interface breaks on the first self-closing tag. YAML is what operators and partners hand over as configuration (mapping tables, fee schedules, code lists) because they will edit it and JSON is hostile to that. And JSON Schema is how you refuse a bad batch before Prisma throws halfway through a 400-row import with the first 180 rows committed.
catalogue.risk: Both package choices are compromises forced by the one-call contract. fast-xml-parser is better maintained but its API is a class, so xml-js is used instead: no publish since 2019, no CVE and no dependencies but also no fixes, and its ergonomics are felt daily — compact mode wraps text as _text and attributes as _attributes, so a read is {{doc.Invoice.Total._text}} and a typo is silent. There is no XSD, Relax NG or namespace resolution, so prefixes stay inside key names and the day a partner moves ns2: to ns3: every binding breaks. ajv is likewise unusable (constructor plus compile), so jsonschema is used: its validate() is a plain function but it implements draft-04 through draft-07, which means a schema written today with $defs, prefixItems or unevaluatedProperties parses and then silently UNDER-validates — the worst failure mode a validator has. Its errors are objects with property/message ('instance.a does not conform'), so per-field form messages are caller work every time, and validating rows individually needs a loop, which Validate Rows works around by wrapping the row schema in an array schema — errors then key on instance[3].field rather than by row. js-yaml's load throws on malformed input instead of returning an error, so every caller needs an exception handler; YAML is for operator-authored config and JSON Schema for untrusted payloads, never the reverse. All three verified requiring and running under Node 20 CJS.

functions.name: Parse XML
functions.description: Parse a document into a compact object — element text under _text, attributes under _attributes, numbers and booleans converted.

functions.name: Parse XML Preserving Order
functions.description: The verbose form, which keeps element order and repeated siblings exactly as they appeared — a statement of transactions, a sequence of line items.

functions.name: Build XML
functions.description: A compact object to an XML string, optionally indented for a document that gets archived and read.

functions.name: Parse YAML
functions.description: A YAML document to an object. Throws on malformed input — wrap it in an exception handler and show the parser's message, which names the line.

functions.name: Write YAML
functions.description: An object back to YAML, sorted and reference-free, for an operator to edit or a config file the deployment commits.

functions.name: Validate Against Schema
functions.description: Check one object against a JSON Schema. Read {{r.valid}} to branch and {{r.errors}} to say what was wrong.
functions.returns: { valid, errors: Array<{property, message, name, argument}> }

functions.name: Validate Rows Against Schema
functions.description: Check every row of a parsed import against one row schema in a single call, so an upload is accepted or rejected whole instead of failing part-committed.

catalogue.name: Print & Correspondence
catalogue.tagline: Decision letters, purchase orders, case files and label sheets that print correctly the first time.
catalogue.why: A back-office app's last step is almost always paper: a decision letter, a PO, a case file for the registry, a sheet of asset tags for the label printer. Today that means a code page per document, margins tuned by trial and error, and the discovery three weeks in that the app's sidebar prints on every page. Because a library compiles INTO the consumer, one PrintDocument wrapper turns the browser's own Print-to-PDF into the correspondence path — and the same components render on screen, so what a clerk previews is what the recipient gets.
catalogue.risk: One bent rule and two real problems. The bent rule: window.print() is a DOM global, which the code-component contract nominally forbids — it is confined to a click handler behind a typeof guard, but a reviewer should agree to that before this ships. The problems: page-break control across a long table is genuinely unreliable between engines (Chrome honours break-inside:avoid, older Safari does not), so a 200-row table will split badly somewhere and needs a tested row cap; and print margins and headers belong to the browser, so anything that must be dimensionally exact — a regulated label sheet, a form with printed boxes — belongs in the built-in PdfExport node, not here. Say plainly what this does NOT do: it produces nothing a workflow can attach to an email. Tailwind has no @page utility and a stylesheet import is not allowed, so the page rule is a literal <style> element in JSX — markup rather than an import, and legal, but worth knowing before someone tries to make it a class.

components.name: PrintDocument
components.description: Wraps content as a physical page: fixes the width, sets the page rule, hides app chrome when printing.
components.notes: The @page rule is emitted as a literal <style> element in JSX; everything else is Tailwind print: variants. Screen preview and print output are the same component, which is the point.

components.name: LetterHead
components.description: Organisation letterhead: mark, address block, contact rules, optionally repeated on every printed page.
components.notes: Repeat is emulated with a print:fixed header band and falls back to first-page-only where the engine ignores it.

components.name: RecipientBlock
components.description: The addressee block, optionally positioned for a DL window envelope.
components.notes: windowEnvelope offsets the block with fixed mm padding so it lands in the window of a standard DL envelope.

components.name: SignatureBlock
components.description: Signatory name, title, date and either a ruled line or a signature image.
components.notes: Held together with break-inside-avoid so a signature never lands alone on a trailing page.

components.name: BarcodeImage
components.description: Displays a barcode or QR code produced by a server action, from SVG markup or a data URL.
components.notes: Always on a white ground with a border ring whatever the theme, because a scanner needs the quiet zone and dark mode makes a code unreadable; the caption underneath does follow the theme. Consumes the barcode library's output rather than encoding anything itself.

components.name: LabelSheet
components.description: A grid of labels — asset tags, case covers, visitor passes — that prints with the app's chrome removed.
components.notes: A CSS grid with print: variants, break-after-page at each page boundary, and dashed crop marks that render only under print. Each cell stacks the code over title and subtitle.

components.name: PageBreak
components.description: Forces or avoids a page break at this point in the document.
components.notes: A thin wrapper over the break-before / break-after / break-inside utilities.

components.name: PrintOnly
components.description: Content that exists only on paper — statutory footnotes, appeal rights, the copy-to list.
components.notes: hidden print:block.

components.name: ScreenOnly
components.description: Content that must never print — navigation, action bars, internal notes.
components.notes: print:hidden. The pair is what stops an internal note reaching an applicant.

components.name: PrintButton
components.description: Opens the print dialog, with a hook to finalise the document first.
components.notes: window.print() inside the click handler only, guarded by typeof window — the one global this library touches.

catalogue.name: Barcodes & QR Codes
catalogue.tagline: QR codes and 1D/2D barcodes as SVG or a data URL, generated inside your own app.
catalogue.why: Inventory, asset registries, case management and visitor systems all print something that gets scanned: an asset tag, a case-file cover, a ticket, a document-verification link. There is no way to make one in Etyma today, so teams paste in a third-party image API — which means every asset number in the estate is sent to someone else's server. This keeps it inside the app: text in, SVG or a PNG data URL out, bound straight to an Image widget or handed to the print library.
catalogue.risk: Nothing here writes a file. A data-URL PNG for a 500-label run is megabytes of base64 held in memory and passed through an action result — fine for one label, wasteful for the batch that is the real use case, and the fix (an AppFile) needs a platform node; prefer the SVG forms, which are small enough to store in a Text column. Both qrcode entry points return promises, which the generator handles because it awaits every CallFunction, but it means these actions are server scope only and a page cannot make a code without a round trip. Decoding is out of scope entirely: reading a scanned barcode needs a camera and a browser decoder, which is neither this library nor an allowed import, so 'scan to look up' stays unserved. bwip-js embeds no fonts for non-Latin human-readable text under the bars, which matters for a bilingual public-sector label. Pin correction worth noting: the received wisdom that bwip-js v4 is ESM-only and must be pinned at 3.4.0 is wrong in both halves — 3.4.0 has NO toSVG at all (only toBuffer), while 4.5.2 requires cleanly from the root under Node 20 CJS and returned real SVG for a code128 in testing. Pin 4.5.2.

functions.name: QR Code SVG
functions.description: A QR code as SVG markup — crisp at any size, small enough to store in a Text column, and what a printed label should use.

functions.name: QR Code Image
functions.description: A QR code as a PNG data URL, which binds directly to an Image widget's src with no component and no file route.

functions.name: QR Code Image Sized
functions.description: The same at a chosen pixel width and error-correction level — raise correction to Q or H for a code printed on something that gets handled.

functions.name: Barcode SVG
functions.description: A 1D or 2D barcode as SVG for a named symbology — code128, ean13, datamatrix, pdf417, gs1-128, interleaved2of5 — with the value printed underneath.

functions.name: Asset Label Barcode
functions.description: A Code 128 barcode at a fixed size that fits a standard 70×37mm label, so every label in the estate comes out identical.

catalogue.name: Business Rules as Data
catalogue.tagline: Approval thresholds and eligibility as JSON a policy owner can change without a release.
catalogue.why: The things that actually change in a line-of-business app are the numbers and the branches: the approval threshold, who a claim routes to, whether an applicant qualifies. Encoded as flow If-nodes, every policy tweak becomes a code change, a release and a change-advisory board. json-logic evaluates a rule expressed as ordinary JSON with a fixed operator set — no eval, no code execution — so the rule can live in an application setting or a lookup-table row and be reviewed by the people who own the policy. In a regulated setting that distinction is the whole argument: a scripting node never passes security review, a declarative rule with a closed operator set does.
catalogue.risk: Judge this on one question: will a policy owner really edit that JSON? If the honest answer is no, it should not ship without a rule-builder component beside it — and then it is a UI library wearing a logic library's clothes. Beyond that, json-logic has no date arithmetic and only cat/in/substr for strings, so anything time-based must be precomputed into the data object by the caller (which is why it pairs with the working-days library and is weaker alone). Rules are unversioned text in a setting, so a bad edit takes effect on the next request with no dry-run and no diff unless the consumer builds one — for an approval threshold that is a genuine production hazard, and Rule Inputs plus a stored copy of the previous rule is the cheapest mitigation. apply returns any, so a rule yielding a string where the flow expects a boolean fails at runtime rather than at build. Verified under CJS: apply({'>':[{var:'amt'},100]},{amt:150})=true and uses_data on the same rule returned ["amt"].

functions.name: Evaluate Rule
functions.description: Apply a JSON rule to a data object. The rule comes from an app setting or a lookup record, the data from the case being decided.
functions.returns: whatever the rule yields — a boolean, a number, a string

functions.name: Decide
functions.description: The matched branch of an if/else rule — the routing target, the approval tier, the approver role — as one value the flow can switch on.

functions.name: Rule Inputs
functions.description: Every field name a rule reads. Check it against the entity before saving a rule, so a renamed attribute is caught at edit time instead of in production.

functions.name: Is Rule
functions.description: Whether a stored value is a well-formed json-logic rule, before it is accepted from a form or an import.

functions.name: Is Truthy
functions.description: json-logic's own truthiness, so a flow branching on a rule's result agrees with the engine that produced it — an empty array is falsy here and truthy in JavaScript.

gaps.name: Lists, Filters & Selection
gaps.tagline: The behaviour around a list page — search, filter chips, sortable headers, selection, paging and saved views — wrapped around the canvas's own table.
gaps.why: This is the largest hole in the catalogue, and two proposed libraries already presuppose it. approval-actions ships a BulkActionBar that "appears when rows are selected" and nothing in the catalogue produces a selection. page-states ships a NoResults whose primary action is Clear filters and nothing produces a filter. Every console in this audience — case queues, claim registers, requisition lists, asset registries — is a table with a search box, two or three filters, a sortable header, a checkbox column and a pager, and today every one of those is hand-wired per page: a page variable per filter, a client action per header cell, a select-all that forgets the ids on page two. These are the behavioural parts only, deliberately: the rows stay in the model's own Table > TableBody > Repeat structure so the designer keeps the page.
gaps.risk: The strongest argument against this is the platform's own: a page is composed from the parts, and a monolithic DataTable would take the body away from the canvas — which is why there is no DataTable here, and why the pieces that remain are awkward in exactly one place. ColumnChooser emits a visible-key list but the canvas's columns are static structure, so honouring it means an If per column and a header the developer keeps in sync by hand; if that proves unbearable in a real build, column visibility is platform work (a Repeat over a column list) and this component should be dropped rather than shipped as a trap. The deeper friction is that filtering and sorting are model decisions: a Query's filters are authored in the flow, so a runtime FilterBar only produces an object the page must translate into inputs its own action already declares — the component cannot close that loop and a developer who expects it to will be disappointed. PaginationBar can rarely show a total, because the generated entity route returns a bare array and sends X-Total-Count only on ?count=1, so an honest total costs a second read and the default has to be Next/Previous on hasMore. There is no virtualisation library on the allow-list, so a selection over 5,000 rows is paged selection or nothing. And selection state living in a page variable means every row emits an event: if that wiring is the real cost, this moves work rather than removing it. If it ships, it should ship merged with approval-actions' BulkActionBar — splitting selection and bulk actions across two library modules guarantees they drift.

components.name: ListToolbar
components.description: The band above a list: search, result count, refresh, density, and a slot for filters and page actions.
components.notes: acceptsChildren, so filters and the page's own primary action are dropped in from the canvas rather than passed as an array the component would have to style. Search debounce is a setTimeout in a useEffect with a cleanup — no lodash — and the component reports the query, never fetches. Result count reads "412 cases" or "51 of 412 shown" and is text-muted-foreground, so it never competes with the primary action.

components.name: FilterBar
components.description: Applied filters as removable chips, with an add-filter popover typed per field.
components.notes: Radix Popover per field with a control chosen by type; the component emits the whole filter object in one onChange so the page runs one action rather than one per field. Clear all appears only above zero applied filters. Chips wrap rather than scroll, because a horizontally scrolled filter row hides applied filters on a phone, which is how users end up staring at an empty list they filtered themselves into.

components.name: FilterChip
components.description: One applied filter as a labelled, removable chip, usable outside the bar.
components.notes: label:value in one chip with a lucide X button carrying an aria-label of "Remove filter <label>" — the chip's own text is not enough for a screen reader when a dozen are applied.

components.name: SortableHeader
components.description: A header cell that emits a sort request — placed inside the canvas's own TableHead.
components.notes: Renders a button inside the cell, sets aria-sort on the parent th through a wrapper element, and cycles asc → desc → none so a user can get back to the default order without reloading. The arrow is a lucide ChevronUp/ChevronDown/ChevronsUpDown triple, the inactive one at 40% opacity so a sortable column is discoverable before it is clicked.

components.name: SelectionCheckbox
components.description: The row and header checkboxes that build a selection in a page variable.
components.notes: @radix-ui/react-checkbox, with the header instance computing indeterminate from selectedIds against the ids on the current page only — and saying so in its title, since 'select all' silently meaning 'this page' is the classic bulk-action incident.

components.name: PaginationBar
components.description: Page size, position and movement, honest about whether a total is known.
components.notes: With totalCount it reads 'Showing 51–100 of 412'; without it, 'Showing 51–100' plus Next/Previous driven by hasMore — because the generated entity route returns an array and a count is a second request. Page size options are bounded by the app's MAX_PAGE_SIZE, which the page passes in rather than the component guessing.

components.name: ColumnChooser
components.description: Which columns are shown, and in what order.
components.notes: Radix DropdownMenu with checkbox items; reordering is up/down buttons per row, not drag, because react-dnd is not an allowed import and a pointer-event reorder is a week of edge cases for a control used twice a year. Required columns render checked and disabled.

components.name: SavedViewsBar
components.description: Named filter-and-sort presets — 'My overdue', 'Awaiting my approval' — as one row of tabs.
components.notes: The component holds no storage: views are rows in the app's own table, so they are shareable, auditable and survive a browser change. A dirty indicator (a dot) appears when the current filters differ from the saved view, which is the difference between a saved view people trust and one they abandon.

components.name: EditableCell
components.description: In-place editing of one cell, for the back-office triage pass where opening each record is the whole cost.
components.notes: Enter or blur commits, Escape reverts, and the cell shows a busy ring rather than an optimistic value — an optimistic edit that the server rejects on a list of 50 rows is unrecoverable confusion. Never edits more than one cell at a time.

gaps.name: Calendars, Agendas & Booking
gaps.tagline: Month grids, day and week timelines, resource rows and bookable slots — hand-built, because every calendar package is off the allow-list.
gaps.why: Scheduling is named in this product's own audience list and the catalogue has nothing for it: MonthPicker is a reporting period, TimePicker is a time input, DatePicker is deferred to the built-in calendar. An inspection roster, a court list, a clinic's appointment book, a licensing officer's site visits, an equipment booking register — each needs a month grid with events on days, an agenda for the next fortnight, a day timeline with overlapping appointments, and a picker of free slots. FullCalendar, react-big-calendar and every scheduler component are network-fetched or unlisted imports, so the only routes available today are an iframe to someone else's calendar or a table of ISO strings. This is the one part of a line-of-business app where the absence of a component means the feature is not built at all rather than built slowly.
gaps.risk: The date arithmetic is the whole risk and there is no date library in the browser. A day timeline built as 24 fixed rows is wrong twice a year in every DST jurisdiction (a 23- and a 25-hour day), so hours must be enumerated from the zone rather than counted, and this is the bug that will reach production because nobody tests in late October. First-day-of-week is not universal and Intl.Locale weekInfo is not implemented everywhere, so it has to be an explicit prop with a documented default rather than a guess, and ISO week numbers — which European public bodies plan by — are a hand-written computation. Overlapping-event layout is a real algorithm (a sweep over start-sorted intervals into columns) and is what separates a calendar from a list with lines. Drag-to-move and drag-to-create are the two gestures users expect from a calendar and react-dnd is forbidden, so either they are hand-rolled on pointer events with the touch and cancel cases handled, or the library ships without them and says so plainly — a calendar you cannot drag on is a legitimate product, an undocumented one is a complaint. There is no virtualisation, so a resource timeline is capped at a page of resources. And the server half is missing: working-days has no holiday calendar and no working-hours clock, so 'the next available slot on a working day' is composed in the caller's flow from a lookup table, which this library cannot do for them.

components.name: CalendarToolbar
components.description: Period label, previous/next/today, and the view switch shared by every surface here.
components.notes: Today is an outline button, not the primary — the primary action on a scheduling page is New booking, and a toolbar that competes with it is the one-primary-action rule broken by a control nobody presses twice.

components.name: MonthCalendar
components.description: A month grid with events on days, out-of-month days dimmed and today marked.
props: events (Array<{id, start, end, title, tone, allDay?}>)
components.notes: A 7-column grid walked as [year, month, day] integers — integers inside, ISO at the edges. Weekday and month names come from Intl.DateTimeFormat; weekStartsOn is a prop because Intl.Locale weekInfo is missing in some engines and defaulting to Sunday is wrong across most of Europe and Asia. Past maxEventsPerDay a '+3 more' button emits the day rather than growing the row, so the grid keeps its shape.

components.name: WeekGrid
components.description: A day or week timeline with hour rows, positioned events and a working-hours band.
components.notes: Hours are enumerated in the supplied zone rather than counted from 0, so a DST day renders 23 or 25 rows instead of silently shifting every event by an hour. Event geometry is inline top/height styles — values, never interpolated class names — and overlaps are laid out by a sweep over start-sorted intervals into columns. Outside working hours the ground is bg-muted, which is how a reader finds the bookable band without reading the labels.

components.name: AgendaList
components.description: What is coming up, as a list grouped by day — the view that works on a phone.
components.notes: Day headings are sticky and compare Intl.DateTimeFormat parts in the supplied zone, never local midnight, so a reader in another office does not see events split at the wrong boundary. This is the fallback the month grid collapses to below sm, so a scheduling page is not a horizontal scroll on a phone.

components.name: ResourceTimeline
components.description: Rows of officers, rooms or vehicles against a run of days, with bars for bookings.
props: items (Array<{id, resourceId, start, end, title, tone}>)
components.notes: Days are grid columns and a bar is a grid-column start and span, so the layout needs no measurement and no ResizeObserver — the trap this repository has already paid for once with a canvas measured before it had width. Weekend columns take a muted ground; capacity over-subscription rings the row destructive rather than stacking bars off-screen.

components.name: SlotPicker
components.description: Bookable slots grouped by day, with taken, held and unavailable states.
components.notes: Buttons in a wrapping grid; taken and blocked slots are disabled with an sr-only reason rather than removed, because a visibly full day tells a caller to try another one and a silently empty day reads as a broken page. Held slots (someone else is mid-booking) are outlined and re-enable when the page refreshes them.

components.name: DateRangePresets
components.description: This week, last 30 days, this quarter, year to date — emitted as a from/to pair.
components.notes: Every boundary is computed by integer arithmetic from the supplied today prop, never Date.now(), so the designer canvas and a snapshot test render deterministically. Custom opens the built-in calendar rather than reimplementing a range picker.

gaps.name: Page & Record Shell
gaps.tagline: The page chrome that is behaviour rather than structure — record headers, a responsive two-pane layout, section navigation, sticky footers and an idle-session warning.
gaps.why: The design gate makes every page declare a layout template — list, detail, form, dashboard, master-detail, settings, inbox — and the catalogue supplies a component for none of them. Most of that is right: a header is Box + Text + Tailwind and belongs to the designer. What is not composable is the behaviour: a master-detail that shows one pane on a phone and both on a laptop with a working back affordance, a long application form whose section nav follows the scroll, a footer that sticks without covering the last field, and a header that gains a shadow only once content is under it. Every one of those is written per app, badly, and the phone case is usually skipped entirely — which for a public-sector caseworker on a tablet is the whole experience.
gaps.risk: This is the proposal most at odds with the platform's own thesis, and half of it should probably be cut. PageHeader and CollapsibleSection are twenty minutes of Box and Text on the canvas, and shipping them as code takes the page away from the designer for no behaviour in return — if this library ships, it should ship as the four behavioural components and nothing else. MasterDetail is the sharpest case: it owns which pane is visible, which is routing state the model already owns through page parameters, so two sources of truth for 'which record is open' will disagree the first time someone deep-links. SectionNav needs an IntersectionObserver against children it does not own, in a designer that mounts components before layout settles — the exact condition this repository has already lost a session to. IdleTimeoutDialog is included because a signed-out-after-n-minutes warning is a security-policy requirement in most of this audience and has nowhere else to live, but it is honestly a stretch for a layout library and it can only warn: the session and its expiry belong to the platform's generated session module, and a component that counts down independently will drift from it. Every slot here depends on acceptsChildren, the least-exercised path in the page designer.

components.name: RecordHeader
components.description: The top of a case, claim or requisition: reference, title, status, the four facts people scan for, and the actions.
components.notes: Facts render as a wrapping row of label-over-value pairs that collapse to two columns on a phone; the reference is font-mono and selectable, because it is the string a user pastes into a ticket. statusSlot and children are slots, so the status badge comes from status-sla and the actions from the page — the header never styles a decision. Sticky adds a border only once the page has scrolled, through a scroll listener on the nearest scroll parent.

components.name: MasterDetail
components.description: List beside detail on a laptop, one at a time on a phone, with a back affordance that actually works.
components.notes: A CSS grid with one breakpoint — no measurement, no ResizeObserver. Below the breakpoint it renders the list until hasSelection, then the detail with a back button that emits rather than calling history, so the page decides whether back means clearing a variable or navigating. With no selection on a wide screen it shows the empty-detail line instead of a blank half-page.

components.name: SectionNav
components.description: Anchor navigation down the side of a long form or a long record, marking where the reader is.
components.notes: An IntersectionObserver over the section ids with a rootMargin biased to the top, falling back to click-only when the observer finds nothing — a nav that highlights nothing is worse than a nav that only navigates. Sections with invalid set carry a destructive dot, which is how a 60-field application form tells someone where the errors are without scrolling.

components.name: StickyFooterBar
components.description: Save, Submit and Cancel pinned to the bottom of a long form without covering the last field.
components.notes: reserveSpace adds matching bottom padding to the scroll container, which is the detail hand-rolled sticky footers always miss and which makes the last field unreachable on a phone keyboard. print:hidden by default, so it never lands on a printed case file.

components.name: PageHeader
components.description: Breadcrumbs, title, description and the page's actions in one band.
components.notes: Included for consistency with RecordHeader and honestly the weakest thing here — it is composable on the canvas, and it earns a code component only through the sticky shadow behaviour.

components.name: CollapsibleSection
components.description: A titled section that folds, with a summary line while closed.
components.notes: Native details/summary, so it is keyboard-operable and printable without a library. Setting invalid forces it open — a collapsed section hiding a validation error is how a form becomes unsubmittable with no visible reason.

components.name: IdleTimeoutDialog
components.description: 'You will be signed out in 2 minutes' — the warning a security policy asks for, with one button to stay.
components.notes: @radix-ui/react-alert-dialog, focus-trapped and not dismissible by clicking away, counting down from a prop the page supplies — the component never owns the clock, because the real expiry is the session token's and two counters will disagree. Announces through role=alertdialog so it is not a silent visual event.

gaps.name: Reporting Statistics
gaps.tagline: Medians, percentiles, spread, trend and banding — the figures an SLA report is made of and lodash does not have.
gaps.why: Every service desk and case-management deployment reports the same numbers to a steering committee, and none of them are a sum or a count: 90th-percentile resolution time, median days to decision, the spread that shows one officer's queue is the problem, the trend line on a twelve-month backlog, and the bands that turn a column of ages into a red/amber/green summary. lists gives sumBy, countBy and maxBy and stops exactly where reporting starts, so today a percentile is a hand-written sort-and-index inside a {{= }} expression, which is where the off-by-one lives. It also closes a real hole in the catalogue as proposed: nothing anywhere turns rows into the number array every one of these functions takes, because lists publishes no map or pluck.
gaps.risk: Judge this against the alternative, which is SQL: these are in-memory over whatever rows the flow already holds, so a percentile over a month of tickets means loading a month of tickets, and past a few thousand rows the honest answer is the ExecuteSQL node with percentile_cont, not this library. Percentile method matters and is not neutral: simple-statistics' quantile interpolates, while an SLA clause that says '90% of cases within 5 days' usually means nearest-rank, and the two disagree on small samples — which is exactly where a monthly report lives. A p90 over eleven cases is arithmetic, not information, and nothing in a one-call action can refuse to compute it. Natural Breaks returns clusters rather than boundaries and is O(n·k), so it is for banding a few hundred values and not a live page. The gap this cannot fill is the cross-tab: status by month, officer by outcome — the shape half of these reports actually want — because a pivot is groupBy then mapValues then sumBy and one CallFunction is one call, so it stays three nodes or an expression. And a catalogue-level hazard this library makes concrete: lodash is now declared by lists, pii and this module, js-sha256 by audit-change and pii — a consumer referencing two of them merges two manifests, and a version disagreement is a build failure a developer did not cause and cannot see the source of. One pin table across the catalogue, or one of them owns each package. Package interop is not verified in this session: check that simple-statistics resolves as named CommonJS exports under Node 20 before pinning.

functions.name: Values Of Field
functions.description: The values of one field across rows, as a plain array. Call it first — every function below takes numbers, not records, and nothing else in the catalogue produces them.

functions.name: Average
functions.description: The arithmetic mean, for a figure whose distribution is known to be sane.

functions.name: Median
functions.description: The middle value — the resolution time to report when three abandoned cases would otherwise drag the average.

functions.name: Percentile
functions.description: The value below which that proportion of cases fall. Pass 0.9 for the p90 an SLA report is written against, and check whether your clause means interpolated or nearest-rank.

functions.name: Standard Deviation
functions.description: How spread the values are — the number that shows a queue is inconsistent rather than slow.

functions.name: Interquartile Range
functions.description: The middle half's spread, and the basis for an outlier rule that does not assume a normal distribution.

functions.name: Trend Line
functions.description: Least-squares fit over paired values, as slope and intercept — is the backlog growing, and how fast.

functions.name: Trend Value At
functions.description: The fitted value at a given x, for projecting the line the chart draws or the month after next.

functions.name: Equal Interval Bands
functions.description: Evenly spaced boundaries across the range, for banding ages or amounts into a fixed number of buckets.

functions.name: Natural Break Bands
functions.description: Boundaries that follow where the data actually clusters, so a banded summary reflects the caseload instead of an arbitrary grid.

gaps.name: Countries, Currencies & Addresses
gaps.tagline: ISO country, subdivision and currency data as server calls — for seeding lookup tables and formatting an address the recipient's post office accepts.
gaps.why: Three concrete things a developer looks for on day one of a registry, a procurement portal or a claims system and does not find here. The country dropdown: identity-validation validates a postcode against a country code and nothing in the catalogue can produce the list of countries to pick from, so it becomes a hand-typed lookup table missing half of Africa. The subdivision list: state, province, emirate, prefecture — required on almost every address form and never available for more than one country. And the printed address: print's RecipientBlock takes addressLines and nothing composes them, so an app that posts a decision letter to Japan prints it in British order. This is also the honest place to put the currency list the money library implies but only exposes one record of.
gaps.risk: The intended use is seeding, not calling. A code list reached through a function call cannot carry the customer's own rows — 'Not stated', a disputed territory an agency does or does not recognise, an internal cost-centre code — cannot be versioned for an audit, and changes under the app when a package is bumped, which for a stored country code is a data-integrity event rather than a bug fix. So these should be called once into a lookup entity the customer then owns, and the docs must lead with that or a developer will call them per request and wonder why a form is slow. Names are English only, which fails the bilingual correspondence this audience produces daily; i18n-iso-countries would fix it and cannot be used, because since v7 its names need registerLocale called first and a one-call action has nowhere to call it — so translated names stay a lookup table the customer maintains. @fragaria/address-formatter is the entry most likely to be unbuildable: its export is an object with a format method and a generator that emits a named import may not reach it, so check the module shape before pinning and drop address formatting rather than shipping something that compiles to undefined. iso-3166-1 and iso-3166-2 are small, quiet packages with no maintenance guarantee and a real staleness cost, since ISO reassigns codes. And the pin hazard is concrete here: currency-codes is already declared by money and libphonenumber-js by identity-validation, so a consumer referencing both this and either of those merges two manifests for the same package. None of these were verified in this session.

functions.name: Country List
functions.description: Every ISO 3166-1 country with its alpha-2, alpha-3, numeric code and English name. Call it once to seed a lookup table, not on every page load.
functions.returns: array of { country, alpha2, alpha3, numeric }

functions.name: Country By Code
functions.description: One country's record from its alpha-2 code, for rendering a stored code as a name.

functions.name: Subdivisions Of Country
functions.description: The states, provinces or regions of one country as ISO 3166-2 codes and names — the second dropdown on every address form.

functions.name: Subdivision By Code
functions.description: One subdivision from its full ISO 3166-2 code, so a stored value renders as a name and a type.

functions.name: Currency List
functions.description: Every ISO 4217 currency code, for a currency picker that agrees with the money library's arithmetic.

functions.name: Currencies Of Country
functions.description: The currencies in use in a country — the default to preselect on an invoice or a claim.

functions.name: Calling Code For Country
functions.description: The international dialling code for a country, for a phone field's prefix and for composing an E.164 number.

functions.name: Dialable Countries
functions.description: Every country the phone metadata knows, so a country picker beside a phone field cannot offer one the validator will reject.

functions.name: Format Postal Address
functions.description: An address object to the line order and casing that country's post office expects — the difference between a decision letter that arrives and one that comes back.
params: address ({ road, city, postcode, state, countryCode, ... })

verdicts.reason: Packages are sound: date-fns 4.1.0 + date-fns-tz 3.2.0 both require() cleanly with ESM interop OFF, all 11 named exports present, formatInTimeZone(2026-09-10T00:00Z,'Asia/Singapore') = '2026-09-10 08:00'. Two real defects. (1) 'To ISO String' is billed as 'the canonical string form for storage' but formatISO is SERVER-TZ-DEPENDENT: I ran it under TZ=Asia/Singapore and got '2026-09-10T08:00:00+08:00' where toISOString() gives '2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z'. The same instant stored from a UTC container and a SGT container yields two different strings — the exact disagreement this library exists to prevent. (2) startOfDay/endOfDay/endOfMonth are server-local, not zone-aware: on a UTC server startOfDay of that instant is 2026-09-09T16:00Z, so 'the left edge of a day filter' is 8 hours wrong for the agency. Also the risk note is wrong in direction: date-fns v4 does not silently misread 'YYYY', it THROWS RangeError('Use `yyyy` instead of `YYYY`') — loud, but an unhandled 500 in a flow with no exception handler.
verdicts.fix: Drop formatISO for a To ISO String built on Date.prototype.toISOString (or document that it emits a local-offset form, not Z). Rename Start Of Day / End Of Day to say they are server-local, or add a timeZone parameter and compose them with To Time Zone. Correct the YYYY note to 'throws' so the docs tell people to handle it.

verdicts.reason: lodash 4.x, CommonJS, all 10 named exports present and type-check against @types/lodash under the export's strict tsconfig. Every function is genuinely one call with positional args — orderBy(rows, fields, directions), groupBy(rows, field), toPairs(grouped) — so nothing needs a loop or a chained call. The stated risks are accurate and honestly weighted: Group By returning a keyed object really does force the two-node Group By → Group Entries dance, and mistyped iteratee fields really do fail silently. No hidden dependency, no ESM problem, no arity mismatch.

No forbidden dependency — DescriptionList, FieldDiffTable, JsonViewer, TreeView, MaskedValue and CopyableValue are all reachable with React + Tailwind + Radix + lucide, and the recursion-via-inner-function workaround for CODE-006 is correct. But every one of these takes a structured prop (items, before/after, nodes, value) and propTypeFor in core/src/codeComponents.ts types Object/Object[] as Record<string, unknown>[]. I compiled a representative DescriptionList against the generated tsconfig and got two hard errors: TS2322 'Type unknown is not assignable to type ReactNode' on {it.label} and on {it.value}. This is not theoretical — CLAUDE.md records the identical defect ('record fields typed unknown where a ReactNode was needed') reaching a real sample export. Every component here needs an explicit narrowing reader, and the entry does not say so. Secondary: the built-in pack already ships table.tsx, data-grid.tsx, item.tsx and field.tsx, so the overlap is larger than 'half of a case screen is not a form' implies.
verdicts.fix: State the narrowing tax in the entry and ship a shared typed reader (e.g. str(v)/node(v) helpers in one component imported as @/components/...) rather than leaving each component to cast. Check DescriptionList and FieldValue against the built-in field.tsx / item.tsx before building both.

verdicts.reason: Buildable exactly as described with no imports beyond lucide: Intl.RelativeTimeFormat carries SlaIndicator's phrasing, SlaMeter is three SVG rects with attribute geometry (correctly kept out of Tailwind), and StatusSummaryBar's flex-grow trick genuinely needs no measurement. color-mix(in oklab, currentColor 12%, transparent) works as a Tailwind arbitrary value provided the spaces are underscored. The self-identified risks are the right ones — the word-to-tone map being a guess about someone else's domain, and SlaIndicator's per-row interval being wasteful in a 200-row table — and none of them is a buildability blocker. Only caveat: counts on StatusSummaryBar arrives as Record<string, unknown> and needs the same narrowing as the other object-prop components.

Verified end to end under CJS with ESM interop off. All 9 date-fns exports present; addBusinessDays('2026-09-11', 5) = 2026-09-18 and v4 does accept the ISO string directly, so the claimed no-parse-step shortcut is real; addMonths(31 Jan, 1) clamps to 28 Feb; addYears(29 Feb 2024, 7) clamps to 28 Feb 2031. Every function is a genuine single call with positional args. The risk note is the most honest in the catalogue — date-fns really has no holiday calendar, date-holidays really is a constructor this contract cannot call, and the fixed Sat/Sun weekend really does exclude Fri/Sat jurisdictions — and it leads with those limits rather than burying them.

The arithmetic is solid and every claimed value reproduced exactly: add('10.00','2.50')='12.50', percent('119.99','9.00')='10.80', format('USD','1234.50')='1,234.50', and the mul('19.99','3')='0.60' trap is real. All 9 money-math exports plus currency-codes.code resolve and type-check. One packaging defect that will break the export install: @types/currency-codes DOES NOT EXIST on npm (npm view returns 404) — currency-codes ships its own index.d.ts instead. If the manifest declares typesSource '@types', npmDevDependencies in callFunctionGenerator.ts will emit '@types/currency-codes' into devDependencies and npm install fails outright. Also worth correcting the risk note in the library's favour: format('JPY','1234.50') returned '1,234', so money-math's formatter does consult the currency's digits; it is only the arithmetic that is fixed at 2dp.
verdicts.fix: Declare currency-codes with bundled types, not typesSource '@types', or the generated app's npm install 404s. Soften the JPY/KRW claim to scope it to arithmetic, since Format Amount already handles 0-digit currencies.

verdicts.reason: Everything here is buildable with no forbidden import, and the design judgements are good (NoResults separated from EmptyState, delayMs to suppress the sub-200ms flash, deterministic skeleton widths instead of Math.random). But the overlap the entry flags as a risk is worse than it admits: I listed packages/core/shadcn/ui and the built-in pack already ships empty.tsx, skeleton.tsx AND spinner.tsx. So EmptyState, SkeletonTable's base and LoadingOverlay's indicator are all rebuilding components a developer already has one click away via Add shadcn/ui Components. The entry's own honest test — 'if the built-in Empty grows props, half of this should be deleted rather than maintained beside it' — is already met today for three of six.
verdicts.fix: Cut EmptyState and LoadingOverlay's spinner down to thin compositions over the built-in empty.tsx and spinner.tsx, and ship only the four the built-ins have no answer for: NoResults, ErrorState, PermissionDenied and the table-shaped SkeletonTable.

verdicts.reason: A flatly false capability claim that will ship a broken intake form. The entry advertises Check Tax Id as covering 'US SSN/ITIN (en-US)'. It does not. I read node_modules/validator/lib/isTaxID.js: the en-US pattern is /^\d{2}[- ]{0,1}\d{7}$/ and the check is enUsCheck = 'are the first two digits a valid IRS campus prefix'. That is an EIN (XX-XXXXXXX), not an SSN (XXX-XX-XXXX). Confirmed at runtime: isTaxID('123-45-6789','en-US') = false, isTaxID('078-05-1120','en-US') = false, isTaxID('457-55-5462','en-US') = false. The only thing that passes is the 9-digit unseparated form ('123456789' = true) — and it passes for the wrong reason, being validated as an EIN. So a US form collecting a dashed SSN rejects every valid one, and one collecting digits silently applies EIN rules. Everything else checked out: isPostalCode('018956','SG')=true, normalizeEmail('A.B+ref@Gmail.com')='ab@gmail.com', formatNumber E.164 works in both call shapes, isValidIBAN mod-97 works, and the throw-on-unsupported-locale trap is real for all three validator functions (isIdentityCard('..','SG'), isTaxID('..','en-SG'), isPostalCode('..','ZZ') all throw).
verdicts.fix: Rewrite Check Tax Id as 'US EIN plus 35 mostly-EU national schemes' and state plainly that SSN/ITIN is NOT covered. Add a Normalise Identifier (strip spaces and dashes) — every other identifier here has a normalise partner and the tax id needs one most, since validator only accepts the unseparated form.

verdicts.reason: Every claimed value reproduced byte for byte: slugify('Ministère de Santé')='ministere-de-sante', transliterate('北京')='Bei Jing', distance('Acme Pte Ltd','Acme Pte. Ltd')=1. The ESM analysis is correct and I verified both halves: with require(esm) disabled, change-case 5.4.4 fails with ERR_REQUIRE_ESM while the pinned 4.1.2 requires cleanly, and 5.x also renames paramCase to kebabCase — so the pin is both necessary and permanent, exactly as stated. All five change-case exports, both transliteration exports and both fastest-levenshtein exports resolve and type-check. The Closest Match hazard is real and correctly called out: I fed it 'zzzzzzzz' against two ministries and it confidently returned 'Ministry of Health'.

Buildable as specified — every field is Intl.NumberFormat plus a controlled input, no date or money library reaches the browser, and the sibling import of @/components/FieldFrame is exactly the local specifier the contract permits. The coerceParam hazard is real (I read it: an empty string coerces to a number, so empty and zero are genuinely indistinguishable without a private draft string). One correction to the reasoning rather than the build: the entry omits DatePicker because 'reimplementing react-day-picker's keyboard and locale handling would be a regression' — but react-day-picker is on CODE_COMPONENT_ALLOWED_IMPORTS and calendar.tsx ships in the built-in shadcn pack, so it can simply be imported. Right outcome (don't build one), wrong reason, and the same misreading blocks nothing else here.

Mechanically sound: detailedDiff returns {added,deleted,updated} as claimed, updatedDiff correctly excludes added keys, canonicalize({b:2,a:1})='{"a":1,"b":2}', sha256 gives 64 hex chars, ulid() gives a 26-char id and decodeTime round-trips it. Audit Id taking zero parameters compiles fine — the generator emits ulid() with an empty arg list, exactly as the crypto library's uuid v4 already does. One factual error in a note presented as verified: the entry states 'ulid exports NO isValid, so an id-format check must be a length-and-charset rule in the flow'. On ulid 3.0.2 isValid IS a named export (typeof = function). Telling developers to hand-roll a charset regex for a check the package ships is how a subtly wrong validator gets written. The hash-chain caveats — no keyed HMAC, chaining done by the caller, and the diff needing a projected record rather than a raw Prisma row — are all correct and correctly weighted.
verdicts.fix: Add an Is Audit Id function over ulid's isValid and delete the 'hand-roll a length-and-charset rule' guidance. Pin ulid explicitly (>=2.4) since the claim is version-dependent.

verdicts.reason: No forbidden dependency and the hard parts are correctly chosen: Intl.RelativeTimeFormat for the phrase with Intl.DateTimeFormat in the title attribute is the right answer given no date library may reach the browser, and comparing DateTimeFormat parts in the supplied zone rather than local midnight is the correct fix for day-grouping. The rail-breaks-at-the-dot detail and the ring-not-border on AvatarGroup are both achievable in Tailwind. Composing InitialsAvatar and RelativeTime into TimelineItem via @/components/<Name> is legal and acyclic. Two caveats already stated honestly: no virtualisation is available so paging is the only answer past a few thousand rows, and the chart-1..5 hash for identity collides with the dataviz ramp. Subject to the same Record<string, unknown> narrowing tax as the other object-prop libraries.

Dependencies check out — @radix-ui/react-alert-dialog is on RADIX_PRIMITIVES in core/src/codeComponents.ts, so DecisionDialog's modal focus trap is legal, as are the Popover for AssigneePicker and the checkbox rows. The strictly-presentational discipline is the right call and is what keeps this from colliding with the workflow engine's Approval and HumanTask nodes. The canDecide hazard is correctly identified and correctly refused a fix: a component genuinely cannot enforce authorisation, and Entity.access plus routeGuard is where that lives. Tone mapping through a static table of full class strings rather than interpolation is the correct Tailwind discipline. Same object-prop narrowing tax on decisions/approvals/comments/candidates.

Three of seven functions are broken as declared, and I reproduced each. (1) Build Delimited Text declares [rows, delimiter, newline] → unparse(a,b,c) fails to COMPILE: TS2554 'Expected 1-2 arguments, but got 3', so the exported app does not build. (2) Parse Delimited Text declares [text, delimiter] → parse(text, ';') compiles but THROWS at runtime: "Cannot create property 'dynamicTyping' on string ';'". (3) Build CSV With Columns declares [rows, columns] → unparse(rows, ['c','a']) compiles, runs, and SILENTLY emits every column in the original order ('a,b,c\r\n1,2,3' instead of 'c,a\r\n3,1') — the worst of the three, because it quietly violates the interface agreement the description promises. papaparse takes ONE config object, not positional options. This is fixable — args are emitted as evaluate(expr, ctx) and action parameters are destructured from ctx (serverActionGenerator.ts:597), so one composed expression can carry a parameter into the object — but as written these three ship broken. parse/unparse themselves, and papaparse 5.4.1 under CJS, are fine, and the wrapper/no-BOM/no-file limits are honestly stated.
verdicts.fix: Rewrite those three so the second argument is a single composed expression, e.g. {{= ({ delimiter: delimiter, header: true }) }} and {{= ({ columns: columns }) }}, and redeclare the params to match. Add a compile check for arity — TS2554 is caught by the export gate but only after a developer has wired the node.

verdicts.reason: Buildable, but built on a false premise and it costs the entry its main justification. The note says 'Radix Popover plus a filtered <ul> — no cmdk'. cmdk IS on CODE_COMPONENT_ALLOWED_IMPORTS (UI_LIBRARIES in core/src/codeComponents.ts), and command.tsx in the built-in shadcn pack already imports it. So the entry hand-rolls a listbox, then correctly identifies the resulting accessibility gap as its own top risk ('a hand-rolled listbox that omits aria-activedescendant and roving focus is a regression in exactly the public-sector settings this targets') — while the library that solves precisely that is available and already vendored. Combobox and MultiCombobox are largely command + popover with a different prop shape. The genuinely absent four — RecordLookup's two-line record rows, TagInput, HierarchySelect, TokenTextArea — are worth building and need no forbidden import.
verdicts.fix: Build Combobox and MultiCombobox over cmdk (or over the built-in command.tsx) instead of a hand-rolled ul, which removes the accessibility risk entirely. Keep RecordLookup, TagInput, HierarchySelect and TokenTextArea as written, and add a request-id guard to RecordLookup so a slow response cannot overwrite a fresh one.

verdicts.reason: The components are all buildable — the Sparkline's fixed viewBox with preserveAspectRatio=none plus vector-effect=non-scaling-stroke is genuinely the right trick, ProgressRing's dasharray/dashoffset maths is correct, and Meter/ComparisonBar/StackedBarStrip need no SVG at all. But the entry's central design decision rests on a claim I disproved: it drops a chart set on the grounds that a charting package is 'not on the allow-list'. recharts IS on CODE_COMPONENT_ALLOWED_IMPORTS (pinned ^3.2.1 in CODE_COMPONENT_DEPENDENCIES) and chart.tsx in packages/core/shadcn/ui imports RechartsPrimitive directly. So the hard parts the entry says it is avoiding — nice ticks, label collision, negative values, irregular time axes — are already solved and shipping, and Sparkline is rebuilding a subset by hand. StatTile, DeltaBadge, ProgressRing, Meter and ComparisonBar remain genuinely novel and worth having.
verdicts.fix: Rewrite the risk note against the real constraint, drop Sparkline in favour of the built-in recharts-backed chart.tsx (or state why a 12-point polyline is still worth its own component), and keep the tile/gauge set, which recharts does not cover.

verdicts.reason: The package interop analysis is right and I verified both halves: marked 18.x fails with ERR_REQUIRE_ESM under CJS while the pinned 12.0.2 requires cleanly, and xss genuinely exposes filterXSS as a named export — it stripped onerror from an and escaped a

The only entry in the catalogue that anticipates the platform's real tax, and it does so precisely: ReviewSummary's note that 'nested items arrive as unknown inside Object[], so the component narrows with a small typed reader rather than casting — strict tsc runs on the export' is exactly the TS2322 unknown-to-ReactNode failure I reproduced against propTypeFor. Everything else is buildable with no forbidden import — native drag events plus a visually hidden file input rather than react-dnd, FileReader per readAs, the static class map for step state rather than bg-${state}, and an inline style width for the progress track. The stated limits are honest and correct: the ~5MB base64 ceiling through a JSON action call is a real wall that only a direct-to-storage upload route fixes, no virtualisation exists for ValidationPreview, and aria-invalid rather than a colour ring is required to pass procurement.

All six maskdata exports resolve under CJS and mask correctly when configured — but two defects, one of them the most dangerous single behaviour in the catalogue. (1) maskJSON2 with no options, or with an options object whose field lists do not match, returns the record COMPLETELY UNCHANGED rather than throwing: I ran maskJSON2({nric:'S1234567D'}) and got {"nric":"S1234567D"} back. Mask Record is sold as 'the one to call before a record reaches a log, an outbound webhook or a support export' — an action that silently emits raw PII on a misconfiguration is far worse than one that fails, and the risk note does not mention it. (2) maskCard('4111111111111111') returns '4111***********1' by default — first four plus last one — while the description promises 'mask a payment card to the last four, the form every receipt and refund screen is expected to show'. A developer trusting the description ships a receipt showing the wrong digits. The Pseudonym For salt caveat, the no-free-text-detection gap and the deprecated maskString are all correctly flagged.

verdicts.reason: No forbidden dependency: SignaturePad is pointer events on a canvas, PhotoGrid and DocumentPreviewDialog are Radix Dialog, AttestationBox is Radix checkbox, RatingScale is lucide Star with fill-current toggled. The SignaturePad risk is the best-calibrated one in the catalogue and the repository's own history backs it — CLAUDE.md records both 'a canvas measured before it had width' as a lost session and the page editor's mount-tick baseline bug, so the ResizeObserver plus redraw-from-value requirement is exactly right rather than defensive boilerplate. The data-URL ceiling, the CSP/X-Frame-Options iframe caveat with download as the assumed path, and the point that ConsentList records a decision without being a lawful-basis engine are all correct. Same object-prop narrowing tax on files/images/purposes/statements.

All three packages verified under CJS and every stated limitation reproduced, including the subtle one: jsonschema silently ignores 2020-12 keywords — validate({b:1}, {...unevaluatedProperties:false, prefixItems:[]}) returned valid:true — so the under-validation warning is real and correctly identified as the worst failure mode a validator has. xml2js compact/verbose, js2xml, js-yaml load/loadAll/dump and the YAMLException on malformed input all behave as described. One trap missing from an otherwise thorough risk note: in compact mode a SINGLE child element becomes an object and repeated children become an array — I got {"_text":"a"} for one <Line> and [{...},{...}] for two — so any binding like doc.Invoice.Line[0] breaks on the one-line invoice, which is exactly the shape a statement or line-item document takes. Also nativeType turned '10.50' into the number 10.5, which collides with the money library's two-decimal-string requirement.

The bent rule is safe on this platform: I read checkCodeComponents in core/src/validation.ts and CODE-001..006 check the default export, allowed imports, unresolved local imports, generated-name collisions, event naming and import cycles — nothing restricts DOM globals, so window.print() behind a typeof guard passes validation and compiles. The @page rule as a literal <style> element in JSX is legal React and the correct workaround given no stylesheet import is allowed; Tailwind v4 ships the print: variant, and w-[210mm]-style arbitrary values compile because the class strings are static and scanned in src/. The entry is unusually honest about scope — it says plainly that it produces nothing a workflow can attach to an email and sends dimensionally-exact work to the built-in PdfExport node. Worth adding: these components also render inside the designer webview, where PrintButton would print the IDE iframe.

Both barcode functions are broken as declared; the QR ones are fine. Barcode SVG declares [value, symbology] → toSVG(a, b) does not COMPILE: TS2554 'Expected 1 arguments, but got 2'. Asset Label Barcode declares [value] → toSVG('ASSET-1') compiles but THROWS at runtime: 'bwipp.undefinedEncoder: bcid is not defined'. bwip-js takes exactly one options object {bcid, text, ...}, so neither can be expressed as positional args. Credit where due: the version correction is right — I confirmed bwip-js 4.5.2 requires cleanly under CJS and toSVG returns a real SVG string synchronously — and the promise claim is right too: serverActionGenerator.ts:207 emits await Promise.resolve(fn(...)), so qrcode's promises are handled. One more to write down: QR Code SVG declares only [text], but qr.toString(text) with no options returns terminal ASCII art, not SVG; the body must pass {{= ({ type: 'svg' }) }}.
verdicts.fix: Pass one composed object to bwip-js: {{= ({ bcid: 'code128', text: value, includetext: true, scale: 3 }) }} for Asset Label Barcode, and {{= ({ bcid: symbology, text: value, includetext: true }) }} for Barcode SVG — legal, since parameters are destructured from ctx. Redeclare the params accordingly and note the {type:'svg'} constant on QR Code SVG.

verdicts.reason: Interop and semantics both verified: all four json-logic-js exports destructure and apply() works standalone without a this binding, which is the thing most likely to have broken here. Values match the claims exactly — apply({'>':[{var:'amt'},100]},{amt:150})=true, uses_data returns ['amt'], is_logic discriminates a rule from a plain object, and truthy([])=false against JavaScript's true, which is precisely why Is Truthy earns its place as a separate function. apply({'if':[...]}) returns the matched branch, so Decide is a genuine single call. The stated risks are the right ones and the entry leads with the one that actually decides the matter — whether a policy owner will really edit that JSON — rather than with the technical caveats. The unversioned-rule production hazard and the any return type are both real and honestly weighted.
